label: Chinese Revolution
pitch:
The Wuchang Uprising of 1911 toppled 2,000 years of imperial rule, but what followed was even more dramatic: Sun Yat-sen proclaimed a republic, Chiang Kai-shek and Mao Zedong fought a decades-long civil war for China's soul, and The Long March forged the Communist movement that would reshape the world's most populous nation.

🔑 Key Facts:
• The May Fourth Movement of 1919 ignited a nationwide awakening of anti-imperialism and modernization that radicalized an entire generation
• The Nanjing Massacre saw Japanese forces kill an estimated 200,000-300,000 civilians in one of WWII's worst atrocities
• People's Republic Founded in 1949 when Mao declared 'The Chinese people have stood up' from Tiananmen
• The Great Leap Forward caused a famine killing an estimated 15-55 million people, the deadliest man-made disaster in history

🤔 Why It Matters: The Chinese revolution created the political system that governs 1.4 billion people today. The Cultural Revolution's scars, the Communist Party's grip on power, and China's rise as a superpower all trace directly to this turbulent era.

🎲 Wild Card: During the Xi'an Incident, Chiang Kai-shek was kidnapped by his own generals and forced to stop fighting the Communists and unite against Japan — a twist of fate that may have saved the Communist Party from destruction.

spans.label: Republic of China
spans.description: The Xinhai Revolution toppled 2,000 years of imperial rule, but the new republic quickly fractured into warlord territories. Sun Yat-sen's nationalist movement and the founding of the Chinese Communist Party set the stage for decades of revolutionary struggle.

spans.label: Nanjing Decade
spans.description: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government nominally reunified China and pursued modernization from its capital in Nanjing. Simultaneously, Chiang waged extermination campaigns against the Communists, who survived the Long March to establish a base in Yan'an.

spans.label: Second Sino-Japanese War
spans.description: Japan's full-scale invasion devastated China, killing an estimated 15-20 million Chinese including the Nanjing Massacre's 200,000-300,000 victims. Nationalists and Communists formed a fragile united front, but the war exhausted the Nationalist government while the CCP expanded in the countryside.

spans.label: Chinese Civil War
spans.description: The Nationalists and Communists resumed full-scale civil war after Japan's surrender, with Mao's forces using guerrilla tactics and land reform to win peasant support. By 1949 the Communists had swept the mainland, and Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan.

spans.label: Mao's China
spans.description: Mao transformed China through radical campaigns including land reform, the Great Leap Forward famine that killed tens of millions, and the Cultural Revolution's decade of political upheaval. China became a nuclear power and opened relations with the U.S., but at enormous human cost.

events.label: Wuchang Uprising
events.description: On October 10, 1911, a bomb accidentally detonated at a revolutionary cell's hideout in Wuchang, forcing exposed soldiers to mutiny on the spot — and within weeks, the chain reaction toppled a dynasty.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The date — 10/10, or the "Double Ten" — became the Republic of China's national day, still celebrated in Taiwan today. The soldiers who mutinied that night were part of the New Army, modern units the Qing themselves had built and drilled on Western models; the dynasty was undone by its own modernization project. What spread wasn't a people's revolution: province after province "declared independence" when local military governors calculated the dynasty was finished and that defecting was safer than dying for a lost cause.

events.label: Sun Yat-sen
events.description: Sun Yat-sen — Cantonese doctor, Christian, Western-educated — spent two decades in exile plotting against the Qing, gave the revolution its ideology, and became the republic's first president for exactly six weeks before being pushed aside by a stronger man.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sun was in Denver, Colorado, when the Wuchang Uprising actually broke out and read about it in a newspaper. He had launched ten failed uprisings against the Qing before the eleventh, accidental one, succeeded without him. He is officially claimed as a founding father by both the Republic of China (Taiwan) and the People's Republic of China — the rare figure both sides of the civil war venerate. He died in 1925, before either the Nationalists or the Communists had won.

events.label: Republic of China Proclaimed
events.description: On January 1, 1912, Sun Yat-sen was inaugurated in Nanjing as provisional president of the Republic of China — the first republic in a major continental Asian state, and the end of a 2,000-year-old political system.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sun chose Nanjing as capital as a deliberate rebuke to Beijing, the Manchu imperial center. The republic was proclaimed while the emperor was still technically on the throne in Beijing, making China briefly governed by two rival governments at once. Sun negotiated with Yuan Shikai for weeks, eventually agreeing to stand aside in exchange for Yuan delivering the Qing abdication — a bargain that handed the republic to its strongest enemy within six weeks of its founding.

events.label: Yuan Shikai Seizes Power
events.description: Yuan Shikai was the Qing general who commanded China's best modern army, brokered the emperor's abdication, then leveraged that position to become president — and ultimately attempted to found a new imperial dynasty himself.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yuan had built the Beiyang Army on the German model, and its personal loyalty to him rather than to the state was the key fact of early republican politics. When the Qing court first dismissed him in 1909 he retreated to his home province to "fish" — everyone understood he was waiting. He declared himself Hongxian Emperor in December 1915; three months later, faced with revolt and abandoned by his own generals, he cancelled the monarchy. He died in June 1916, officially of kidney failure, after just 83 days as a self-proclaimed emperor no one recognized.

events.label: Warlord Era
events.description: After Yuan Shikai's death in 1916, China's nominal national government became a fiction — real power shifted to regional generals with private armies, each taxing and conscripting the territory they could hold. The period lasted until the Nationalist reunification of 1928.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The era's Chinese name, junfa ("military cliques"), captures the personal, patron-client nature of these armies — loyalty ran to individual commanders, not to China. The Beijing government remained internationally recognized and collected customs revenue the whole time, meaning foreign loans and tariff money flowed to whichever faction held the capital. At the same time, Sun Yat-sen's rival Nationalist government in Guangzhou contested Beijing's legitimacy, leaving China with two governments, neither able to govern.

events.label: New Culture Movement
events.description: A revolt of young Chinese intellectuals in the 1910s–20s against two thousand years of Confucian tradition, arguing that China's weakness came not from a shortage of guns but from a civilization-wide cage — and that the cure was science, democracy, and a completely new culture.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The movement's founders were almost all classically trained in the very tradition they attacked — Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, and Hu Shi had all mastered the Confucian canon before turning on it. It also produced China's first generation of women writers and editors, as the push to write in everyday spoken Chinese opened publishing to people who had never studied the classics. The movement unfolded primarily through a handful of magazines and university lecture halls rather than street protest — its radicalism was literary before it was political.

events.label: May Fourth Movement
events.description: On May 4, 1919, roughly three thousand students from Peking University and other Beijing colleges marched on Tiananmen to protest the Versailles sellout of Shandong — and the arrests that followed triggered the first successful mass-action reversal of a Chinese government decision in the modern era.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The protest turned violent when students reached the home of Cao Rulin, the minister they blamed for the secret Shandong deal: they beat the diplomat Zhang Zongxiang who happened to be there and burned Cao's house down. The government arrested 32 students that day, then hundreds more — which backfired catastrophically, triggering sympathy strikes by Shanghai merchants and dockworkers that froze the Yangtze trade. Within a month Beijing had backed down, freed the students, dismissed the officials, and refused to sign Versailles — the first time urban mass action had overturned a state decision in China's modern history.

events.label: Chinese Communist Party Founded
events.description: In July 1921, a dozen delegates representing perhaps fifty Marxists across all of China held the First Congress of the Chinese Communist Party in a Shanghai girls' school — and finished the meeting on a tourist boat after the police got suspicious.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tourist-boat finale on South Lake near Jiaxing has become so iconic that the boat is now a national museum piece, with replica congresses reenacted for Party officials. The founding congress was so small that two of its twelve-odd delegates were actually Comintern agents, not Chinese members — meaning Moscow had proportional representation at the moment of birth. Mao Zedong attended as a delegate from Hunan, but played no leading role; the dominant figures were Chen Duxiu (elected Secretary-General in absentia, since he couldn't safely attend) and the Comintern representative Henk Sneevliet, a Dutch communist.

events.label: Lu Xun
events.description: Lu Xun (pen name of Zhou Shuren) was the greatest writer of modern China — a physician-turned-author whose savage short stories in vernacular Chinese diagnosed traditional society as a system of cannibalism dressed up as virtue.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Lu Xun gave up medicine after watching a crowd of Chinese onlookers passively photograph the execution of a Chinese man by Japanese soldiers, concluding that healing bodies was useless if the national spirit was sick. His 1918 story "Diary of a Madman" — the first major prose work published in vernacular Chinese — borrowed its frame from Gogol but made its central metaphor wholly Chinese: a man who reads "benevolence, righteousness, truth" in the old books but sees only the characters for "eat people" between the lines. He died in 1936 before the worst of what followed, which is one reason every faction — Nationalists, Communists, liberals — could later claim him.

events.label: Northern Expedition
events.description: The Northern Expedition (1926–1928) was the Nationalist military campaign that marched out of Canton, smashed the warlords one by one, and reunified China under the Kuomintang — succeeding faster than anyone expected because Communist organizers ran ahead of the army, paralyzing warlord rear areas with strikes and peasant uprisings.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The National Revolutionary Army began the campaign massively outnumbered on paper, but warlord armies were poorly motivated and routinely defected or surrendered. The expedition covered roughly 1,000 miles (1,600 km) in under two years. Chiang Kai-shek stepped down as NRA commander briefly in August 1927 during the Wuhan-Nanjing split, went into exile in Japan, then returned to finish the campaign — taking Beijing in June 1928.

events.label: Chiang Kai-shek
events.description: Chiang Kai-shek was the military commander who won control of the Kuomintang after Sun Yat-sen's death, led the Northern Expedition to reunify China, then governed the Republic for two decades before losing the civil war and retreating to Taiwan, where he remained president until his death in 1975.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Chiang had trained at the Imperial Japanese Army Academy in Tokyo and made a study trip to the Soviet Union in 1923, giving him firsthand knowledge of both future adversaries. He was born in Zhejiang province in 1887 and outlasted nearly every peer of his revolutionary generation, dying at 87 in Taipei. Despite losing the mainland, he held onto Taiwan's UN Security Council seat until 1971, insisting his government was the legitimate ruler of all China.

events.label: Shanghai Massacre
events.description: On April 12, 1927, Chiang Kai-shek's forces and Green Gang gunmen turned on their Communist allies in Shanghai, killing union workers and CCP members in coordinated street-by-street raids over several days — the blow that destroyed the urban Communist Party and ended the First United Front.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Green Gang (a Shanghai criminal syndicate that controlled the docks, opium trade, and labor rackets) provided the muscle for the initial disarming of workers, giving Chiang plausible distance at first. Shanghai's bankers and industrialists, who had bankrolled the KMT's advance, had made Communist neutralization a condition of their support. Similar anti-Communist purges followed in cities across Nationalist-held China within weeks; surviving CCP members fled to the countryside, beginning the shift in revolutionary strategy that led directly to Mao's eventual dominance.

events.label: Nanjing as National Capital
events.description: In 1928 Chiang Kai-shek established the Nationalist capital at Nanjing (meaning 'Southern Capital'), launching a decade of modernization — the 'Nanjing Decade' — that would be cut short by Japanese invasion in 1937.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Nanjing had served as China's capital during the early Ming dynasty (1368–1421) before the court moved to Beijing, so the choice carried historical weight as a reassertion of Chinese sovereignty independent of the northern power centers. The Nanjing government built modern roads, a national bank system, and a professional civil service — real reforms — but never controlled more than parts of the country, with warlords still ruling in the west, Communists building bases in the southeast, and Japan entrenching in the northeast.

events.label: Mao Zedong
events.description: Mao Zedong was the peasant-born revolutionary who outmaneuvered every rival to lead the Communist Party from 1935, commanded the campaign that defeated Chiang Kai-shek in 1949, and then ruled the People's Republic until his death in 1976.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mao was born in 1893 in Shaoshan village in Hunan to a prosperous peasant family — his father was a grain merchant, not a poor peasant, which complicated later hagiography. He was one of the thirteen delegates at the founding congress of the Chinese Communist Party in 1921. Despite holding party leadership from the Zunyi Conference onward, he had no formal head-of-state title until 1954, when he became Chairman of the PRC; before that his power ran through the party chairmanship rather than state office.

events.label: The Long March
events.description: In October 1934, around 100,000 Red Army soldiers and party officials broke through Nationalist lines and retreated roughly 6,000 miles (10,000 km) to a new base in the northwest — a year-long ordeal that killed most of them and became the founding epic of Communist China.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The army that set out numbered close to 100,000; only about 8,000 survived to complete the march. The official Chinese account claims the march covered 25,000 li (roughly 8,000 miles), but historians who retraced the full route put the actual distance considerably lower — the inflated figure was part of the myth-building. Women were officially banned from the march but a small number of female cadres, including Mao's wife He Zizhen, made the journey anyway.

events.label: Xi'an Incident
events.description: In December 1936, the Manchurian general Zhang Xueliang kidnapped Chiang Kai-shek at Xi'an and held him for two weeks, forcing Chiang to agree to stop the civil war and form a united front against Japan — a deal negotiated with Communist Zhou Enlai in the room.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Chiang had flown to Xi'an specifically to order Zhang Xueliang and fellow general Yang Hucheng to launch a final offensive to wipe out the Communists; instead, their soldiers surrounded his villa at dawn on December 12, 1936, and Chiang reportedly fled in his pajamas and hid barefoot on a cold hillside before being captured. Zhou Enlai flew to Xi'an to negotiate, and the Communists pushed for Chiang's release rather than his trial or execution — calculating, correctly, that Chiang was more valuable alive as an anti-Japanese leader. Zhang Xueliang escorted Chiang back to Nanjing and was immediately placed under house arrest, where he remained for over fifty years.

events.label: Marco Polo Bridge Incident
events.description: A nighttime skirmish on July 7, 1937 between Japanese and Chinese troops near a centuries-old stone bridge outside Beijing spiraled in weeks into a full-scale invasion — the eight-year war that would reshape China entirely.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The bridge (Lugouqiao in Chinese) had stood since the 12th century, and Marco Polo described it in the 1200s as the finest in the world. The incident itself began when a Japanese soldier went briefly missing during night maneuvers and his unit demanded to search a nearby Chinese town — the Chinese refused, shots were exchanged, and neither side could stop what followed. The 29th Army defending the area was equipped with traditional Chinese broadswords alongside modern rifles, a detail that captures exactly how mismatched China was going into this fight.

events.label: Nanjing Massacre
events.description: After Shanghai fell and Japanese forces took the Nationalist capital Nanjing in December 1937, they carried out weeks of mass killing and mass rape of civilians and prisoners — an atrocity that remains one of the defining wounds in modern Chinese memory.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The death toll — somewhere between 200,000 and 300,000 by Chinese and Allied war-crimes tribunal estimates — is one of the most politically charged numbers in twentieth-century history: a strain of Japanese nationalist writing has minimized or denied it, which remains a live diplomatic wound between the two countries today. A group of Western civilians and diplomats who stayed behind created a "Safety Zone" in the city that sheltered roughly 200,000 Chinese refugees from the worst of the killing. The massacre became the foundational evidence for the argument, repeated by every Chinese leader since Mao, that a weak China invites destruction.

events.label: Yan'an Soviet Base
events.description: The 8,000 survivors of the Long March arrived in the dusty loess hills around Yan'an in October 1935 and turned this impoverished northwestern backwater into the Communist Party's capital and laboratory for the next decade.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yan'an sits in the Loess Plateau of Shaanxi province — a landscape of soft, eroded yellow earth where the population lived in cave-homes carved directly into the hillsides, and where the Communists did too, including Mao himself. It became a destination for thousands of idealistic young students and writers who trekked there from the cities, transforming what had been a survival refuge into an intellectual center. The party used the Yan'an years to run the 'Rectification Campaign' (1942–44), a mass ideological discipline exercise that made Mao's interpretation of Marxism the only permitted one.

events.label: Yan'an Talks on Literature
events.description: Mao's talks established that art and literature must serve the revolution and the masses, defining cultural policy for decades.

events.label: People's Republic Founded
events.description: On October 1, 1949, Mao Zedong stood at the Tiananmen gate in Beijing and proclaimed the People's Republic of China, declaring 'The Chinese people have stood up' — five words that framed a century of foreign humiliation, from the Opium Wars through the Japanese invasion, as finally, definitively over.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Chinese Communist Revolution had been running in some form since 1927 — a 22-year arc from the Shanghai Massacre to the proclamation. The founding of the PRC became a model studied by revolutionary communist movements worldwide, from Vietnam to Cuba to Angola. The phrase 'the Chinese people have stood up' (Zhongguo renmin zhan qilai le) does not appear verbatim in the speech Mao actually delivered at Tiananmen — it comes from an earlier address to the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference the day before, on September 30.

events.label: Land Reform Campaign
events.description: Between 1950 and 1952 the CCP redistributed roughly 40 percent of China's cultivated land from landlords to poor peasants — the largest transfer of property in human history — while organizing mass "struggle sessions" that killed hundreds of thousands to over a million landlords.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The campaign gave hundreds of millions of peasants a plot of land for the first time in their lives, which is why it created real popular gratitude even among those who later suffered under collectivization. Landlord status was defined not by total wealth but by the share of income derived from "exploitation" rather than labor — a definition flexible enough to catch village moneylenders, clan leaders, and anyone with a grudge pointed at them. The deliberate implication of ordinary villagers in the killings was part of the design: by making peasants the executors of the violence, the Party bound them politically to the new order.

events.label: China Enters Korean War
events.description: In October 1950 Mao sent hundreds of thousands of troops — officially called "Chinese People's Volunteers" to avoid a formal declaration of war — across the Yalu River into Korea, driving UN forces back down the peninsula in one of the most dramatic reversals in American military history before the war ground to a stalemate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The initial PVA force was 250,000 men drawn from six corps of the PLA, transferred wholesale but given a different name to preserve the legal fiction that China was not at war with the United States. About 3 million Chinese military and civilian personnel served in Korea over the course of the conflict. The PVA's nominal commander was General Peng Dehuai — who would later clash fatally with Mao over the Great Leap Forward (Chapter 11). Mao's own eldest son, Mao Anying, was killed by a US airstrike in Korea in November 1950.

events.label: Hundred Flowers Campaign
events.description: The Hundred Flowers Campaign (1956–57) invited intellectuals to criticize the party and help correct its errors — a brief, extraordinary opening that produced a flood of frank dissent before being abruptly reversed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The campaign's name came from a classical poem: "Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend." Criticism built slowly at first because people were afraid, but by spring 1957 it had become a torrent — university students posted wall newspapers attacking party officials, and prominent intellectuals questioned whether one-party rule was legitimate at all. Whether Mao designed the whole thing as a trap to identify critics or was genuinely shocked by the scale of dissent remains one of the genuinely contested questions in PRC historiography, with credible historians on both sides.

events.label: Great Leap Forward
events.description: In 1958 Mao Zedong launched a nationwide campaign to industrialize China through collective willpower alone — and instead produced the largest famine in human history, killing an estimated 15–55 million people between 1958 and 1962.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The death toll range is unusually wide because the Chinese government suppressed the data for decades; more recent scholarship puts the figure around 30–46 million excess deaths. Mao explicitly framed the campaign as a race to overtake Britain in industrial output within fifteen years — a goal he believed sheer revolutionary mobilization could achieve without capital, technology, or technical expertise. The campaign ran for four years before Beijing quietly abandoned its targets, but it was never publicly acknowledged as a failure during Mao's lifetime.

events.label: Sino-Soviet Split
events.description: The ideological alliance between China and the Soviet Union — the two great communist powers — collapsed through the late 1950s and early 1960s, as Mao condemned Khrushchev's softening of Stalinist doctrine as a sellout of revolution, while Moscow saw Beijing as dangerously reckless about nuclear war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The split had a concrete nuclear dimension: the Soviets had promised to share atomic bomb technology with China in 1957, then withdrew the offer in 1959 as relations deteriorated — pushing China to develop its own bomb independently (it succeeded in 1964). The break also scrambled Cold War alignments in ways neither superpower expected: the US eventually found common cause with China against the USSR, the geopolitical logic that Nixon and Kissinger would exploit a decade later.

events.label: Cultural Revolution
events.description: From 1966 to 1976, Mao Zedong unleashed the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution, a decade of purges, mass violence, and ideological terror that shattered China's institutions and killed hundreds of thousands to over a million people.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Cultural Revolution was triggered partly by Mao's alarm at de-Stalinization in the Soviet Union — he feared the same 'betrayal' would happen in China after his death. Schools and universities across the entire country simply closed for several years, meaning a full generation of Chinese youth received no formal education. The movement ultimately purged not just enemies but Mao's own most loyal followers, as Red Guard factions turned on each other with increasing violence.

events.label: Red Guard Movement
events.description: Red Guards were student paramilitary groups mobilized by Mao in 1966 to attack teachers, intellectuals, and 'class enemies,' smashing cultural heritage and running public humiliation sessions (called 'struggle sessions') before being forcibly disbanded in 1968.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Red Guard units had no central organization — dozens of competing factions in a single city would fight each other over ideological purity while all claiming loyalty to Mao. They acquired weapons from military stockpiles, and by 1967 some factions were conducting artillery battles in the streets. The Guards destroyed an estimated 4,922 of Beijing's 6,843 registered cultural heritage sites in a matter of months during the Red August of 1966.

events.label: Quotations from Chairman Mao
events.description: Lin Biao compiled Chairman Mao's sayings into a small red pocket book, distributing billions of copies to make it the most-printed book of the 20th century and the physical totem of the Mao cult.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At the Cultural Revolution's peak, failing to carry the Little Red Book in public was itself dangerous — it was effectively mandatory. The book was published in 66 languages and distributed to foreign communist movements worldwide, becoming a global symbol of revolutionary politics in the 1960s. Lin Biao's introduction to the book praised Mao's thought as 'a compass for action' and 'a spiritual atom bomb.'

events.label: Zhou Enlai
events.description: Zhou Enlai served as China's premier from 1949 until his death in January 1976 — the indispensable administrator, diplomat, and quiet damage-limiter of the Mao era, a man who somehow navigated every purge, every campaign, and every catastrophe without losing his head or Mao's confidence.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Zhou had been the political director of the Whampoa Military Academy in the 1920s when Chiang Kai-shek was the commandant — meaning he knew Nationalist China's entire officer class personally before both sides tried to kill each other. He was the chief Chinese negotiator at the 1954 Geneva Conference on Korea and Indochina, putting the PRC on the world diplomatic stage for the first time. The spontaneous mass mourning after his death — crowds filling Tiananmen Square unbidden — told Mao and the radicals exactly how much more popular Zhou was than they were.

events.label: Nixon Visits China
events.description: President Richard Nixon's eight-day visit to Beijing in February 1972 — the first by a sitting US president — ended 23 years of diplomatic non-recognition and produced the Shanghai Communiqué, a document that acknowledged Taiwan's disputed status without resolving it in a formula both sides have lived with ever since.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Nixon arrived on February 21 and met Mao the same day in a meeting that lasted barely an hour — Mao was already visibly ill and rambling — but the symbolism was seismic. The visit produced the Shanghai Communiqué, in which the US notably did not endorse Taiwan independence and China did not demand immediate unification, a deliberate diplomatic ambiguity that has defined cross-strait relations for five decades. Full normalization between Washington and Beijing didn't happen until 1979 under Carter, seven years after the handshake.

events.label: PRC Takes UN Seat
events.description: On October 25, 1971, the UN General Assembly voted to seat the People's Republic of China and expel the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek's Taiwan government, handing Beijing the permanent Security Council seat with veto power that Taipei had held since 1945.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The resolution — UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 — framed the move as restoring China's "lawful rights," implying Beijing had always been the legitimate holder and Taiwan merely a usurper. The vote was 76 to 35 with 17 abstentions, a more lopsided result than Washington expected; several US allies voted for expulsion. Taiwan has not held a UN seat since, and the resolution is still cited by Beijing as international law settling the question of Taiwan's status.

events.label: First Chinese Nuclear Test
events.description: On October 16, 1964, China detonated its first atomic bomb at the Lop Nur desert test site, becoming the world's fifth nuclear power and asserting strategic independence from both the United States and the Soviet Union.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The test — codenamed Project 596 — used uranium-235, not plutonium, which surprised Western intelligence analysts who expected a simpler design. It came just three years after the Soviet Union withdrew all its nuclear advisers in 1961, meaning China completed the bomb essentially from scratch. China announced the test publicly the same day, declaring it would never be the first to use nuclear weapons — a 'no first use' pledge it maintains to this day.

events.label: Tiananmen Incident of 1976
events.description: On April 4–5, 1976 — the traditional Qingming Festival day for honoring the dead — hundreds of thousands of Beijing residents spontaneously gathered in Tiananmen Square to mourn Zhou Enlai, turned it into a protest against the Gang of Four, and were forcibly dispersed, with Deng Xiaoping blamed and purged for the second time.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The gathering was triggered when authorities began removing wreaths and poems left at the Heroes' Monument for Zhou, which enraged mourners who saw it as an attack on Zhou's memory by the radicals. The protest was the first large-scale unauthorized political demonstration in Tiananmen Square since 1949 — thirteen years before the more famous 1989 protests that would end in very different circumstances. The Gang of Four pinned the organization of the protest on Deng, giving them the pretext to purge him again; after Mao's death and the Gang's arrest, the incident was officially rehabilitated as a "revolutionary action."

events.label: Death of Mao Zedong
events.description: Mao Zedong died on September 9, 1976, at age 82, after years of deteriorating health from what was likely amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), ending the twenty-seven-year era of the founder-state and triggering a succession fight that was resolved within weeks.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The government ordered a week of national mourning, with memorial services broadcast nationwide and crowds numbering in the millions. Mao's body was embalmed against his explicit wish for cremation — a decision made by the leadership to preserve his symbolic presence — and placed in a crystal sarcophagus in a mausoleum built in Tiananmen Square within a year of his death. His designated successor Hua Guofeng, chosen precisely because he was unthreatening, moved against the Gang of Four within 27 days of Mao's death, well before any faction could consolidate power.

events.label: Soong Sisters
events.description: The three Soong sisters married into China's most powerful families, shaping Republican-era politics, finance, and revolution.

events.label: Barefoot Doctors Program
events.description: The Barefoot Doctors program trained millions of minimally-educated farmers and villagers as basic health workers, pushing rudimentary medical care — vaccinations, hygiene, childbirth — into China's vast rural interior for the first time.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: By the 1970s there were roughly one million barefoot doctors nationwide, giving China more rural health workers per capita than most developing nations. The program contributed to life expectancy rising from roughly 35 years in 1949 to over 65 years by the late 1970s — one of the fastest such gains in recorded history. The World Health Organization later cited the barefoot doctors model as a template for primary healthcare in developing countries, influencing the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration on global health.

events.label: Great Hall of the People
events.description: Built in just ten months as one of the Ten Great Buildings, the Great Hall became the seat of China's legislature on Tiananmen Square.

events.label: Yangtze River Flood Control
events.description: Catastrophic Yangtze floods killed over 30,000 people, prompting massive dam-building and flood control infrastructure projects.

events.label: Simplified Chinese Characters
events.description: In 1956 the PRC officially promulgated a set of simplified Chinese characters, reducing the stroke count of hundreds of common characters to make reading and writing easier to learn for the largely illiterate rural majority.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The simplification project drew on centuries of informal shorthand forms that calligraphers and merchants had already been using; the government standardized and extended them rather than inventing from scratch. The first round in 1956 simplified 515 characters; a more radical second round attempted in 1977 was so unpopular it was withdrawn within two years. Today the simplified/traditional split maps almost exactly onto the political divide: mainland China and Singapore use simplified; Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau use traditional.

events.label: Destruction of Religious Sites
events.description: The Red Guards' 'Destroy the Four Olds' campaign — targeting old ideas, culture, customs, and habits — produced a wave of religious and cultural destruction across China, smashing temples, churches, mosques, and irreplaceable artifacts.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In Tibet, nearly all of the region's roughly 6,000 monasteries were destroyed or severely damaged during the campaign, with much of the destruction carried out by Tibetan Red Guards as well as Han Chinese. Confucius's tomb at Qufu — a site of continuous veneration for over 2,400 years — was desecrated and its grounds ransacked. The campaign was explicitly modeled on previous CCP anti-superstition drives but was far more violent and comprehensive than anything before it.

events.label: State Atheism Enforced
events.description: The CCP promoted atheism and restricted religious practice, nationalizing church properties and expelling foreign missionaries.

events.label: Tongmenghui Founded
events.description: In Tokyo in 1905, Sun Yat-sen merged a cluster of rival anti-Qing exile groups into a single underground organization — the Tongmenghui, or Revolutionary Alliance — giving China's fragmented revolutionaries a unified structure and program for the first time.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The founding meeting was held on August 20, 1905, in Tokyo, which was then home to thousands of Chinese students studying abroad — the Meiji-era Japanese model of rapid modernization had made it a magnet for reformers who wanted to do the same for China. Song Jiaoren, who would later build the Tongmenghui into the Kuomintang and be assassinated for it, was one of the co-founders. The organization operated as a secret society with rituals and oaths, not a conventional political party.

events.label: Three Principles of the People
events.description: Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People — nationalism (end foreign domination), democracy (representative government), and people's livelihood (vague land reform) — became the founding ideology of the Republic and later the official doctrine of KMT rule.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The three principles were deliberately elastic: "people's livelihood" was close enough to socialism to appeal to reformers but vague enough not to scare landowners. Sun drew on an unusual mix of sources — Marxism, classical Chinese utopianism, and the land-value tax ideas of American economist Henry George. Under KMT rule the principles achieved near-religious status, a formal state ideology, and Sun himself was elevated into a cult of personality. The Communists later claimed Sun as a proto-socialist; the Nationalists claimed him as a proto-democrat.

events.label: Abdication of the Qing
events.description: On February 12, 1912, a six-year-old boy named Puyi signed an abdication edict in the Forbidden City, ending not just the Qing dynasty's 267-year reign but the entire institution of imperial monarchy — an unbroken chain of dynasties stretching back over two thousand years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The abdication edict was written and signed on behalf of Puyi by his regent, not the child himself. The Qing were Manchu — an ethnic minority from northeast China — who had conquered a Han Chinese empire in 1644 and ruled for nearly three centuries as a foreign dynasty. The revolution that finally toppled them had been building for a decade and was triggered not by a popular uprising but by a bomb that went off by accident. The new Republic's first president held office for exactly six weeks.

events.label: Kuomintang Founded
events.description: Song Jiaoren rebuilt the revolutionary Tongmenghui into a proper political party — the Kuomintang (Nationalist Party, KMT) — to contest China's first national elections in 1912, and won them decisively.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The KMT won roughly 45% of seats in China's new parliament, making it by far the largest party — a genuine electoral mandate in a genuinely contested election. Song built his appeal on the gentry, merchants, and landowners, pitching constitutional government as the protection of property and order. He was 30 years old when he was shot, on his way to Beijing to form a government that could have constitutionally constrained Yuan Shikai. The KMT Sun eventually led from exile was a reorganized, Soviet-advised version of the original; the party Song built was a different animal.

events.label: Assassination of Song Jiaoren
events.description: Song Jiaoren — the KMT's parliamentary architect and its most effective politician — was shot at Shanghai's railway station in March 1913 while en route to take office as premier, dying two days later at thirty years old.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Song had just led the KMT to a sweeping victory in China's first democratic elections. The money trail from his killer led to Yuan Shikai's own premier; historians have concluded Yuan was behind it, though no court ever tried him for it. Song's death ended the first attempt to make the republic work through ballots rather than guns — and set the template for how every subsequent threat to military power in China would be handled. He was the last Chinese republican politician who genuinely believed elections alone could check a general.

events.label: The Second Revolution
events.description: After Song Jiaoren's assassination, KMT-aligned southern provinces rose against Yuan Shikai in the summer of 1913; the revolt was crushed in two months, and Sun Yat-sen fled into exile in Japan for a second time.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The "Second Revolution" is the name applied retrospectively; at the time it was simply called the southern revolt. Seven provinces declared against Yuan, but they had no common army, no unified command, and no foreign support — Yuan had all three. The whole thing collapsed in about two months. Yuan's response was to ban the KMT outright, expel its members from parliament, and eventually dissolve parliament altogether. Sun's return to Japan was his third exile from China; he had spent most of his adult life outside the country he was trying to govern.

events.label: The Twenty-One Demands
events.description: In January 1915, Japan secretly delivered 21 demands to Yuan Shikai's government that would have handed Japan control over Manchuria, Shandong, and ultimately the Chinese government itself — effectively converting China into a Japanese protectorate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Japan timed the demands deliberately: Europe's great powers were locked in the First World War and couldn't intervene in Asia. Yuan stalled for months, then leaked the demands to the press to generate international embarrassment for Japan — it worked enough to get the most extreme provisions dropped, but not enough to save him. The day Yuan accepted a reduced version was declared by Chinese students the "Day of National Humiliation" (May 9), an anniversary that was observed for decades and fed directly into the nationalism that would drive the May Fourth Movement in 1919. Japan's ambassador delivered the demands in person on January 18, 1915.

events.label: Yuan Shikai's Empire
events.description: In December 1915, Yuan Shikai declared the Republic a mistake and proclaimed himself emperor of a new dynasty — a catastrophic misreading of his own country that triggered immediate nationwide revolt and destroyed everything he had built.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yuan was reportedly encouraged by advisers, including his own son and Japanese counselors who told him the Chinese people wanted a strong emperor. His new dynastic era name was "Hongxian" (Glorious Constitution), chosen with some irony. Even generals who had been personally loyal to him declined to fight hard for his throne: the monarchy's prestige had been the one thing the 1911 revolution genuinely destroyed. He cancelled the monarchy on March 22, 1916 — after exactly 83 days — and died three months later, officially of uremia.

events.label: National Protection War
events.description: When Yuan declared himself emperor, the southern province of Yunnan revolted first, in December 1915, and the uprising spread — the National Protection War ended the monarchy within months and, when Yuan died in June 1916, removed the last man holding China together.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The revolt was led by Cai E, a general who had been Yuan's own military governor in Yunnan — the betrayal by trusted subordinates was what made it fatal. The war lasted from December 1915 to July 1916, running nearly concurrent with Yuan's self-cancellation of the throne. Yuan's death left the Beiyang Army with no single commander and no loyalty to the state — it immediately began fracturing into the competing regional factions that would spend the next decade fighting each other in the warlord era.

events.label: The Beiyang Army Splits
events.description: Yuan Shikai built the Beiyang Army in 1895 as China's first modern force — Western-drilled, Western-equipped, loyal to him personally. When he died, that personal loyalty evaporated and the army split into the warlord factions that defined the next decade.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Beiyang Army was established not as a national force but as Yuan's private power base, which is precisely why it could not survive him intact. Its officer corps had trained together and knew each other, so the factions that emerged were built on those preexisting relationships of patronage and shared schooling. The army's influence on Chinese politics outlasted the warlord era itself — historians trace its shadow all the way to 1949.
