events.label: The Warlord Cliques
events.description: The Beiyang Army's fragments coalesced into named cliques — Zhili, Anhui, and Fengtian being the main three — each fighting the others for the right to occupy Beijing and claim the legitimacy of the recognized national government.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The cliques were not ideological factions but personal networks bound by loyalty, money, and sometimes marriage — closer to feudal houses than political parties. Holding Beijing mattered because the foreign powers that had signed treaties with China still recognized whoever sat there, giving the winning faction access to customs revenues and international loans. Control of the capital changed hands through both battle and bribery, with generals routinely buying off rivals' subordinates rather than fighting pitched engagements.

events.label: Zhang Zuolin and the Fengtian Clique
events.description: Zhang Zuolin rose from rural banditry in Manchuria to become the most powerful warlord in China's northeast, playing Japanese ambitions against Beijing rivals for over a decade — until Japanese officers, deciding he had become a liability, blew up his private railway car in 1928.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Zhang's assassination by Japanese Kwantung Army officers (the Huanggutun Incident) was carried out without Tokyo's approval, marking the first time Japanese military officers in China acted unilaterally against their own government's orders — a pattern that would escalate into the full invasion of Manchuria three years later. Despite running the industrially richest region in China, Zhang never controlled the Beijing government until 1927, when he was declared Generalissimo — a title he held for less than a year before his death.

events.label: The Manchu Restoration Attempt
events.description: In July 1917, the pigtailed conservative warlord Zhang Xun marched his troops into Beijing under the guise of mediating a political dispute and restored the eleven-year-old former emperor Puyi to the throne — an episode that lasted exactly twelve days before republican forces reversed it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Manchu Restoration ran from July 1 to July 12, 1917 — Puyi's second abdication came before his twelfth birthday. Despite the royalist optics, nearly all of the putschists were ethnic Han Chinese, not Manchus. In a detail that belongs in any history of modern warfare, republican troops dropped small bombs from an airplane on the Forbidden City during the counter-offensive, one of the earliest aerial bombardments ever conducted in Chinese history.

events.label: China Enters World War I
events.description: China entered World War I on the Allied side in August 1917 — not with soldiers, but by sending roughly 140,000 laborers (the Chinese Labour Corps) to dig trenches, haul shells, and bury the dead on the Western Front, in exchange for a promised seat at the peace conference.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Chinese Labour Corps served under both British and French command and endured the same conditions as combat troops — including artillery fire and the 1918 influenza pandemic — yet were kept segregated behind the lines and largely forgotten in postwar memory. China's calculation was specific: by joining the Allies, it expected to recover the German-leased territory in Shandong province, which Germany had bullied from the Qing in the 1890s. That expectation was shattered at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, when the Allies handed Shandong to Japan instead, detonating the May Fourth Movement.

events.label: Beijing versus Guangzhou
events.description: Sun Yat-sen refused to accept the warlord-controlled Beijing regime as the legitimate Republic, and from 1917 onward established a series of rival governments in Guangzhou (Canton) in the south, contesting Beijing's claim to speak for China.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sun's southern governments went through three distinct phases between 1917 and 1922, each time collapsing when local Guangdong warlords proved unwilling to stay under his authority. The third attempt, begun in 1923, took a different approach — reorganizing the Kuomintang along Leninist party-discipline lines with Soviet help — and became the direct foundation for the Northern Expedition that finally ended the Warlord Era in 1928.

events.label: The Treaty-Port Economy
events.description: While the countryside suffered under warlord taxation and conscription, China's foreign-run treaty ports — Shanghai above all — boomed during World War I as European competition vanished, creating a Chinese-owned industrial and commercial economy and an urban working class that had not existed a generation earlier.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Treaty ports operated under extraterritoriality (the legal principle that foreign nationals living there answered to their own courts, not Chinese law), meaning the fighting and economic chaos outside their borders rarely penetrated inside. The boom created a new Chinese middle class of factory owners, bankers, and professionals alongside a large industrial proletariat concentrated in a few cities — exactly the social formations Marxist theory predicted would produce revolutionary politics, and exactly the audience the Communist Party targeted in the early 1920s.

events.label: Yan Fu and Social Darwinism
events.description: The scholar Yan Fu (1854–1921) translated Thomas Huxley, Herbert Spencer, John Stuart Mill, and Adam Smith into Chinese in the late 1890s and early 1900s, introducing Social Darwinism and Western liberal thought to a generation of Chinese reformers who read national weakness as a life-or-death evolutionary crisis.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yan Fu was trained as a naval officer at the Fuzhou Shipbuilding School and later studied in Britain, which gave him both the technical English to translate and a firsthand sense of Western industrial power that made the translations urgent rather than academic. His rendering of Huxley's "Evolution and Ethics" framed China's situation as a struggle for national survival in a world that eliminated the unfit — a reading that radicalized the generation of students who would launch the May Fourth Movement and, later, the Communist Party.

events.label: The Rural Crisis
events.description: Across the warlord years and beyond, China's peasant majority — roughly 80 percent of the population — faced overlapping claims from landlords, warlord tax collectors, local garrisons, and moneylenders, producing the structural poverty and dispossession that the Communist Party would later turn into its most powerful political weapon.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A Chinese peasant in the early 1920s might owe land taxes collected years in advance by a warlord who needed campaign funds, rent to an absentee landlord, interest to a rural moneylender, and be subject to conscription by any army passing through. Tenancy rates in some provinces exceeded 50 percent of farmland, meaning the farmer who worked the soil owned none of it. This was not a new condition but a worsening one — warlord competition multiplied the layers of extraction that the Qing system had already imposed.

events.label: Missionary Schools and Colleges
events.description: Christian missionary schools and colleges built by American, British, and European churches across China's cities trained a Westernized, English-literate educated class — the very generation that led the nationalist and revolutionary movements, even as those movements turned against foreign influence.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: By the 1920s, missionary institutions included full universities (Yenching, St. John's in Shanghai, Ginling College for women) with curricula indistinguishable from their Western counterparts. The paradox was sharp: the institutions built to spread Christianity ended up producing China's most ardent nationalists and, in several cases, Communist organizers, because the Western education they provided included Western political philosophy alongside the Bible. Many of the student leaders of the 1919 May Fourth protests had been educated in exactly these schools.

events.label: New Youth Magazine
events.description: Chen Duxiu's magazine *New Youth* (also called *La Jeunesse*), founded in 1915 and running until 1926, was the house organ of the New Culture Movement — the place where the slogans "Mr. Science" and "Mr. Democracy" were hammered out issue by issue.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Chen Duxiu launched the magazine in Shanghai, not Beijing, and its first print runs were small enough to fit in a suitcase; it only became a phenomenon after Peking University adopted it as essential reading. The magazine later shifted left so sharply that by the early 1920s it was functioning as a de facto organ of the nascent Communist Party. Its bilingual French subtitle — *La Jeunesse* — was a deliberate signal that the editors saw themselves as part of a global youth revolt, not a purely Chinese one.

events.label: The Vernacular Language Revolution
events.description: Philosopher and diplomat Hu Shi, trained at Cornell and Columbia under John Dewey, led the campaign to replace classical Chinese (*wenyan*) with vernacular (*baihua*) as the language of serious writing — a reform that made mass literacy structurally possible for the first time.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hu Shi's famous "eight principles" of literary reform, published in *New Youth* in 1917, were deliberately modest in tone — he framed them as practical writing tips, not a revolution — yet their implications were vast: a literature readable by people who had not spent a decade memorizing the classics could, in theory, reach 400 million people rather than a few thousand officials. He spent the rest of his career arguing for gradual liberal reform against the revolutionary left, famously telling radical students to "study problems, not isms" — a slogan that made him deeply unfashionable after 1919 and permanently principled.

events.label: The Shandong Decision
events.description: At the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, China — an Allied victor — arrived expecting the return of Germany's former colonial rights in Shandong province, only to discover the conference intended to hand those rights to Japan, honoring secret wartime deals the bankrupt Beijing government had already made.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The betrayal was compounded by the revelation that the Chinese delegation in Paris already knew about the secret agreements — the "Twenty-One Demands" Japan had forced on China in 1915, and a 1918 loan deal that ceded Shandong rights as collateral — but had been instructed by Beijing to sign anyway. The delegation ultimately refused to sign the Versailles Treaty, the only Allied power to do so. The Shandong issue was eventually resolved at the 1922 Washington Conference, when Japan agreed to return the territory under American and British pressure — but the three-year delay had already radicalized a generation.

events.label: Li Dazhao and Chinese Marxism
events.description: Li Dazhao, head librarian of Peking University, was the first prominent Chinese intellectual to publicly embrace the Bolshevik Revolution — and his Marxist study circle is where the young library assistant Mao Zedong first became a convinced communist.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Li Dazhao was unusual among early Chinese Marxists in arguing that China's peasants, not its tiny urban working class, could be the revolutionary force — a heresy against orthodox Marxism that would later become Mao's signature. He co-founded the CCP in 1921 but remained in Beijing as a secret organizer rather than a public party figure. In April 1927, after Chiang Kai-shek's massacre of Communists in Shanghai, Li was arrested by the warlord Zhang Zuolin at the Soviet embassy compound in Beijing — technically Soviet territory — and executed by slow strangulation, the method reserved for major criminals.

events.label: The Comintern Comes to China
events.description: The Communist International (Comintern), Moscow's global organization for exporting revolution, sent agents to China with money, organizational blueprints, and a strategy — transforming scattered study circles into the Chinese Communist Party and, simultaneously, rebuilding Sun Yat-sen's Nationalist Party along Leninist lines.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Comintern's most consequential decision in China was to tell the tiny CCP not to build independently but to join the much larger Nationalist Party (the Kuomintang) as individual members — a strategy called the "United Front" — on the theory that the Nationalists were the revolutionary engine and the Communists would steer it from inside. The chief Comintern architect of this strategy was Henk Sneevliet (code name "Maring"), the Dutchman who also attended the CCP's founding congress. The Comintern existed until 1943, when Stalin dissolved it as a gesture to his wartime Western allies.

events.label: The Kuomintang Reorganized
events.description: Between 1923 and 1924, with Soviet guidance from Mikhail Borodin, Sun Yat-sen rebuilt the Kuomintang from a gentlemen's club into a disciplined Leninist mass party complete with a propaganda department, a party press, and a party-controlled army — the organizational template that both the Nationalists and later the Communists would use to rule China.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The reorganized KMT adopted the Soviet model wholesale: centralized party cells, mandatory ideological training, and commissars embedded in military units to ensure political loyalty. Before the reorganization the KMT had won elections but couldn't enforce its authority because it had no armed force; the Soviet model fixed that structural weakness directly. The KMT went on to rule mainland China from 1928 to 1949 and Taiwan under martial law until 1987.

events.label: The Anti-Christian Movement
events.description: Student nationalists attacked Christianity and mission schools as instruments of imperialism, fusing anti-religion and anti-foreign feeling.

events.label: The Science and Philosophy of Life Debate
events.description: A 1923 public debate over whether science could guide human life crystallized the New Culture faith that science would save China.

events.label: The Woman Question
events.description: May Fourth intellectuals made women's liberation a flagship cause — attacking footbinding, arranged marriage, and the Confucian ideal of the obedient daughter-in-law as symptoms of the same cultural sickness that was killing China.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The May Fourth era produced China's first wave of women writers, journalists, and university students — New Youth published women's essays and the 1920s saw women enrolled at Peking University for the first time. The debates were not just abstract: hundreds of young women cut their hair short (a radical public statement), refused arranged marriages, and in several celebrated cases ran away from home to study, treating themselves as the living proof that the old system was breakable. The movement's feminist gains were later subordinated first to Nationalist and then to Communist party priorities, which tended to frame women's liberation as a side effect of class revolution rather than a goal in itself.

events.label: The Sun-Joffe Manifesto
events.description: The Sun-Joffe Manifesto was the 1923 joint statement between Sun Yat-sen and Soviet envoy Adolph Joffe that formally opened the door to Soviet aid for the Kuomintang and set the terms of Communist cooperation inside the KMT.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The manifesto explicitly stated that Soviet-style communism was not suitable for China given its conditions — a face-saving clause that let Sun accept Soviet help without looking like he had surrendered his party to Moscow's ideology. In exchange, the Soviets sent money, weapons, and Comintern advisers including the strategist Mikhail Borodin. Joffe had previously negotiated with Japanese leaders before arriving in China, and the manifesto was signed in Shanghai in January 1923.

events.label: Whampoa Military Academy
events.description: Whampoa Military Academy, founded near Canton in 1924 with Soviet funding, was the school that trained the officer corps of both the Nationalist and Communist armies — and where Chiang Kai-shek and Zhou Enlai, future enemies, first worked side by side.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The academy ran an unusually short curriculum — the first class graduated in under six months — so that officers could be deployed quickly to the coming Northern Expedition. Soviet advisers brought the Red Army's model of embedding political commissars alongside military commanders, teaching cadets that ideological commitment was as important as battlefield skill. Graduates from Whampoa ended up on both sides of every major conflict from the Northern Expedition through the 1949 civil war.

events.label: The First United Front
events.description: The First United Front (1924–1927) was the Soviet-brokered alliance in which Chinese Communists joined the Nationalist Kuomintang as individuals — a 'bloc within' — to defeat the warlords and reunify China together, before the partnership exploded in a massacre.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The alliance was formally called the KMT-CCP Alliance and was primarily organized by the Comintern (the Soviet-run international communist body) over the objections of many Chinese Communist Party members who feared being swallowed. Together the two parties created the National Revolutionary Army that launched the Northern Expedition in 1926. The arrangement lasted just four years before Chiang Kai-shek's Shanghai Massacre in April 1927 destroyed it entirely.

events.label: Death of Sun Yat-sen
events.description: Sun Yat-sen died of liver cancer in Beijing on March 12, 1925, leaving behind a famous deathbed will urging comrades to keep striving and a Kuomintang with no agreed heir — the vacuum Chiang Kai-shek would fill by controlling the army.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sun had traveled to Beijing for peace negotiations with northern warlords when he fell ill; the trip itself was a sign of how precarious his southern Canton government remained. His will's phrase — 'the revolution is not yet successful; comrades must still strive' — became a ritual invocation at Kuomintang ceremonies for decades. He was 58 years old and had spent nearly 30 years in repeated failed revolutions before the KMT finally held real territory.

events.label: The May Thirtieth Movement
events.description: British police killing protesters in Shanghai in 1925 set off nationwide strikes and boycotts that swelled both KMT and Communist ranks.

events.label: The Canton Coup
events.description: The Canton Coup (Zhongshan Incident) of March 20, 1926 was Chiang Kai-shek's sharp preemptive strike against Communist and Soviet influence inside the KMT — arresting Soviet advisers and Communist political officers — that consolidated his personal command just before the Northern Expedition.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The coup's name comes from the gunboat Zhongshan (named for Sun Yat-sen's courtesy name), which was moved to a provocative position near Canton under murky circumstances that Chiang used as his pretext. The Comintern, desperate to preserve the alliance before the military campaign north, accepted humiliating terms: Communists were barred from holding top KMT posts and a list of all CCP members inside the KMT had to be submitted to Chiang. It was a preview of the full 1927 betrayal — just calibrated to keep Soviet guns flowing a little longer.

events.label: The Peasant Movement
events.description: From 1925 to 1927 Communist organizers built peasant associations across southern China's countryside; Mao Zedong's 1927 Hunan report — arguing that the land-hungry peasantry, not the urban working class, was the revolution's real engine — was the heretical idea that would eventually win him China.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mao's report, 'Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan,' was written after he spent January and February 1927 visiting five counties on foot. He described peasant committees seizing land, trying landlords in village courts, and demolishing the old rural power structure with a ferocity he called 'a hurricane.' Orthodox Marxism held that industrial workers, not peasants, made revolutions — Mao's inversion of that formula put him at odds with the Soviet-advised party mainstream for years, but it was the insight that shaped the Long March, the Yan'an base, and the 1949 victory.

events.label: The Shanghai Workers' Uprising
events.description: In March 1927, Communist-led workers launched an uprising that seized control of the Chinese-administered parts of Shanghai, handing the city to the approaching Nationalist army — only for Chiang Kai-shek to repay them with a massacre weeks later.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The April 12 Shanghai Massacre that followed was explicitly anti-communist: Chiang's forces, working with the Green Gang criminal syndicate that controlled Shanghai's docks and labor rackets, turned on their CCP allies in coordinated dawn raids. The workers who had just delivered Shanghai were disarmed, arrested, and shot. The death toll in Shanghai and the subsequent purges across Nationalist China ran into the thousands, and the urban Communist Party was effectively destroyed as an organized force.

events.label: Mikhail Borodin
events.description: Mikhail Borodin was the Comintern's top agent in China from 1923 to 1927, the man who rebuilt the Kuomintang from a loose network of notables into a disciplined Leninist party with a political department, party press, and its own army.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Borodin's real name was Mikhail Gruzenberg; 'Borodin' was the alias he used for undercover work. Before China he had operated as a Comintern agent in Mexico, Turkey, and Britain (where he was briefly arrested). When the United Front collapsed in 1927, he fled China overland through the Gobi Desert and returned to Moscow, where he was later arrested during Stalin's purges and died in a labor camp in 1951.

events.label: The Collapse of the United Front
events.description: By mid-1927, even the rival left-Kuomintang government at Wuhan — which had tried to keep the Soviet alliance alive after Chiang's Shanghai purge — gave in and expelled the Communists, collapsing the First United Front entirely and stranding the Comintern's China strategy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Wuhan government had been set up by the KMT's left wing under Wang Jingwei as an alternative to Chiang's Nanjing faction, and it initially condemned the Shanghai Massacre. But Wuhan's own military commanders were also turning against the Communists, and by July 1927 Wang Jingwei's government expelled the CCP and ended Soviet ties. The Comintern emissary M.N. Roy had fatally shown Wuhan leaders secret Moscow instructions revealing that the Communists planned to take over the left-KMT from inside — destroying any remaining trust.

events.label: Nanchang and the Autumn Harvest Uprising
events.description: In the second half of 1927 the Communist Party launched three armed uprisings in rapid succession — Nanchang, the Hunan countryside, and Canton — and lost all three, forcing the survivors into the hills.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Nanchang Mutiny of August 1, 1927 is still the official founding date of the People's Liberation Army — the PRC celebrates it as Army Day every year. Mao's Autumn Harvest Rising was launched on September 7 in Hunan and Jiangxi; he had hoped for a coordinated peasant and worker offensive but the force disintegrated under Nationalist counterattack within days. The Canton Commune in December lasted barely three days before being drowned in blood, killing thousands of participants and bystanders.

events.label: The Northern Expedition Completed
events.description: The Northern Expedition concluded in June 1928 when Nationalist forces took Beijing and the last northern warlords submitted to Kuomintang authority, giving China nominal political unification for the first time since 1916 — with the new capital at Nanjing.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The submission of Zhang Xueliang (son of the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin, who had just been assassinated by Japanese officers) was a crucial but deeply fragile moment: he accepted Nanjing's nominal authority while keeping his own army intact in Manchuria. Japan's Kwantung Army had killed the elder Zhang specifically to prevent him submitting to Nationalist control, and the 'unification' left Japan holding Manchuria's railways and a permanent foothold — foreshadowing the 1931 invasion.

events.label: The Jiangxi Soviet
events.description: The Chinese Soviet Republic — headquartered in the Jiangxi mountains and known as the Jiangxi Soviet — was a functioning Communist mini-state with its own government, army, currency, and land reform program, running from 1931 to 1934.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The capital was set at Ruijin, a small town in southeastern Jiangxi chosen precisely because it was poor, remote, and hard for Nationalist forces to reach. The CSR formally claimed authority over 18 provinces and 4 counties — an absurd overreach on paper, but its actual territory was a patchwork of disconnected mountain bases. Land redistribution was the policy that mattered most on the ground: taking fields from landlords and giving them to poor peasants gave the Red Army a constituency that would feed it, hide it, and die for it.

events.label: Zhu De and the Red Army
events.description: Zhu De was the Nationalist officer who defected to Mao in 1928, co-founded the Red Army, and became its supreme commander — the military brain behind the guerrilla doctrine that would eventually win the civil war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Zhu De came from a remarkably different background than most Communist leaders: he was already in his early forties when he joined the party, had studied in Germany, and had commanded conventional Nationalist forces. His military partnership with Mao was so total that cadres referred to them as "Zhu-Mao" as if they were a single person. He held the title Commander-in-Chief of the Red Army (and later the People's Liberation Army) for decades, making him the longest-serving top commander in the CCP's military history.

events.label: The Encirclement Campaigns
events.description: Between 1930 and 1934, Chiang Kai-shek launched five successive military campaigns to destroy the Jiangxi Soviet; the first four were repulsed using guerrilla tactics before the fifth finally broke the Communist stronghold.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The first four campaigns failed for a consistent reason: Nationalist commanders sent large columns deep into mountain terrain the Red Army knew intimately, and the Communists destroyed them one piece at a time — a textbook demonstration of Mao's "lure deep, annihilate in detail" doctrine. The fifth campaign was fundamentally different in concept: German military advisors (including Hans von Seeckt, architect of the post-Versailles Reichswehr) persuaded Chiang to build a grid of thousands of small concrete blockhouses linked by roads, advancing the ring slowly inward rather than lunging. It worked because it turned the Communists' mobility advantage into a liability — there was nowhere to maneuver.

events.label: The Mukden Incident
events.description: On September 18, 1931, Japanese officers blew up a small section of their own railway near Mukden (modern Shenyang) and blamed Chinese saboteurs — the false-flag pretext for Japan's seizure of all Manchuria within months.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The explosion was embarrassingly weak: it failed to destroy the track, and a train passed over the damaged section minutes later. That didn't matter — the Kwantung Army (the Japanese force stationed in Manchuria) launched its invasion the same night, and Tokyo's civilian government, which had not authorized the operation, found itself unable or unwilling to rein in its own officers. Japan installed the deposed Qing emperor Puyi as nominal ruler of the new puppet state Manchukuo five months after the incident; the League of Nations condemned the seizure but imposed no sanctions, and Japan simply walked out of the League in 1933.

events.label: The Nanjing Decade
events.description: The ten years Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government ruled from Nanjing (1927–1937) — a period of genuine modernization that never quite controlled the country it claimed to run.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: GDP grew at roughly 3.9 percent a year through the 1930s, and per capita income crept upward — real numbers, not propaganda. But the government's tax base was almost entirely urban customs and excise revenue; the countryside, where most Chinese lived, contributed little and received less. Historians now frame the decade as a period of Chinese conservatism rather than revolution: the Nationalists built state capacity without attempting the kind of social transformation — land reform above all — that might have secured rural loyalty.

events.label: The New Life Movement
events.description: Chiang's 1934 campaign blended Confucian morality, Christianity, and military discipline to remake citizens' behavior from the top down.

events.label: The Futian Incident
events.description: The Futian Incident of December 1930 was a bloody internal purge inside the Jiangxi Soviet, in which Mao's faction tortured and executed hundreds of its own soldiers and cadres on accusations of being enemy agents.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The trigger was Mao's order to purge the Jiangxi Action Committee on the pretext of alleged ties to the 'Anti-Bolshevik League' — a vague accusation that could be pinned on almost anyone. A battalion mutinied against the purge, freed prisoners, and briefly established a rival leadership, which Mao then suppressed with further violence. The incident is historically important less for its immediate death toll than for what it reveals about method: coerced confessions, guilt by association, and the annihilation of internal critics using ideological labels — all techniques that would recur at much larger scale in Yan'an in the 1940s and nationwide after 1949.

events.label: The Fifth Encirclement
events.description: The Fifth Encirclement Campaign (1933–34), devised with German military advice, abandoned frontal assault in favor of a slowly tightening ring of concrete blockhouses — and it worked, strangling the Jiangxi Soviet into a do-or-die breakout.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The blockhouse strategy required building an estimated 14,000 small fortified posts linked by new roads across rough mountain country — a logistical achievement that reflected the Nationalists' growing state capacity. The Communist leadership compounded the problem by dismissing Mao's guerrilla doctrine and insisting on conventional positional defense to hold territory; this decision, made by Soviet-trained leaders who had sidelined Mao, consumed the Red Army's manpower in set-piece battles it could not win. By autumn 1934 the Soviet's territory had shrunk by roughly half and supplies were running critically short — the Long March was the only remaining option.

events.label: The Battle of Xiang River
events.description: Forcing the Xiang River in late 1934 against waiting Nationalist armies, the Red Army lost more than half its strength — dropping from over 80,000 troops to around 30,000 in a matter of weeks — a catastrophe that destroyed the credibility of the Soviet-backed leadership running the march.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Xiang River crossing was the bloodiest episode of the entire Long March, with some estimates putting Red Army dead at over 30,000 in the battle alone. The slow-moving column, burdened with machinery and equipment, was predictable enough that Nationalist commanders had days to prepare their positions. The disaster directly triggered the Zunyi Conference two months later, at which Mao outmaneuvered the discredited leaders who had ordered the suicidal crossing.

events.label: The Zunyi Conference
events.description: In January 1935, surviving Communist leaders met in a captured house in Zunyi town and effectively sacked the Comintern-backed military advisers who had wrecked the army at the Xiang River, shifting military command to Mao Zedong — the moment that launched his four-decade grip on power.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The conference was so politically sensitive that it went completely unacknowledged in official Chinese history until the 1950s, and detailed descriptions weren't published until the fiftieth anniversary in 1985. Mao didn't emerge as undisputed leader on the spot — he was made a member of the Standing Committee and took charge of military planning, but consolidated full authority gradually over the next two years. His chief opponent at the meeting, German Comintern adviser Otto Braun, stayed with the march but lost all real influence.

events.label: Crossing the Dadu River
events.description: The Red Army's crossing of the Dadu River at Luding Bridge in May 1935 — by the official account, twenty-two volunteers swinging hand over hand across bare iron chains under machine-gun fire — became the most celebrated (and most disputed) hero story of the Long March.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Luding Bridge is a 330-foot (100-meter) iron chain suspension bridge built in 1706 under Emperor Kangxi, with thirteen chains and wooden planks — the planks had been removed before the battle. Historians including Sun Shuyun, who interviewed surviving participants, found evidence the far bank was lightly or not at all defended, raising serious questions about whether the famous assault actually happened as described. The bridge itself still stands and is now a national monument and tourist site.

events.label: The Snow Mountains and the Grasslands
events.description: After the snow-capped mountains came something worse: a vast, freezing, trackless high-altitude swamp with no food and no paths, where men drowned in mud and died of exposure in numbers that may have surpassed every battle of the Long March combined.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The grasslands — the Zoige (Ruoergai) Plateau in what is now Sichuan — sit at around 11,000 feet (3,400 meters) elevation and are a maze of peat bogs disguised under grass, where a step off solid ground could mean sinking without trace. The army took roughly a week to cross, surviving almost entirely on wild plants, leather belts, and whatever grain they had carried in. The snow mountains crossed just before included Jiajin Mountain, whose pass sits above 15,000 feet (4,600 meters) — several soldiers who sat down to rest on the way up never got back up.

events.label: The Split with Zhang Guotao
events.description: When Mao's battered column met the larger Fourth Front Army under rival Zhang Guotao in mid-1935, the two leaders deadlocked over direction and authority; Mao went north, Zhang went west, and Zhang's subsequent military disasters left Mao without a serious challenger for the rest of his life.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Zhang Guotao's Fourth Front Army actually outnumbered Mao's force at the time of their meeting, giving him a plausible claim to overall command. His western route ended in catastrophe when his forces were shattered by the Muslim Ma clique cavalry in Gansu — of roughly 80,000 soldiers who took the western route, fewer than 20,000 survived. Zhang eventually defected to the Nationalists in 1938, retired to Canada in 1968, converted to Christianity, and died in Scarborough, Ontario in 1979.

events.label: The December 9th Movement
events.description: On December 9, 1935, thousands of Beijing students poured into the streets demanding that Chiang Kai-shek stop spending his armies fighting Communists and start fighting Japan — the most significant mass protest in China since the May Fourth Movement of 1919.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The protests were partly organized through underground Communist Party networks operating in the universities, though they tapped genuine student fury that required no external direction. The December 9th Movement spread to dozens of other cities within weeks. It put Chiang under enormous public pressure at precisely the moment his commanders in the north — men like Zhang Xueliang, whose Manchurian homeland Japan had seized — were already questioning why they were being ordered to fight Chinese instead of Japanese.

events.label: Red Star Over China
events.description: The American journalist Edgar Snow's reporting from Yan'an gave the Communists a sympathetic global image and a heroic Long March narrative.

events.label: The Second United Front
events.description: The Nationalists and Communists, who had been trying to destroy each other for a decade, agreed in 1937 to stop fighting long enough to resist Japan — a marriage of necessity that was more a ceasefire than a real alliance.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In practice the United Front functioned more like a non-aggression pact than any kind of coordinated military effort — the two parties never merged commands, shared intelligence, or planned joint operations in any meaningful way. Communist forces were folded into the National Revolutionary Army on paper (as the Eighth Route and New Fourth Armies) but kept their own officers, territory, and party structures completely intact. Both sides used the war years to build their own strength for the civil war they both knew was coming the moment Japan was defeated.

events.label: The Battle of Shanghai
events.description: From August to November 1937, Chiang Kai-shek threw his best German-trained divisions into a brutal urban battle for Shanghai — a fight that destroyed the modern core of his army but denied Japan its predicted quick victory.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The battle ran from August 13 to November 26, 1937 — over three months — and is considered by some historians the first true battle of World War II, predating the European war by nearly two years. Japanese war planners had predicted China would collapse in three months; Shanghai alone took that long and cost both sides staggering losses. Chiang's calculation was cold: sacrifice the best army China had to prove to the world (and especially to potential Western allies) that China would fight, not fold.

events.label: The Fall of Wuhan
events.description: The four-and-a-half-month Battle of Wuhan in 1938 was the largest and bloodiest engagement of the entire war — and when the city fell, the Nationalist government made its long retreat to Chongqing deep in the interior.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: More than one million Nationalist troops defended Wuhan across multiple provinces under Chiang Kai-shek's direct command, assisted by Soviet volunteer pilots (the USSR was supplying China before the United States was). The battle was the last major Nationalist offensive effort before the war settled into a grinding stalemate; after Wuhan fell, Japan controlled China's coast and major cities but could never pacify the vast countryside. The Soviet volunteers are a largely forgotten piece of the story — Stalin supported Chiang, not the Communists, in the early war years.

events.label: The 1938 Yellow River Flood
events.description: In June 1938, Nationalist engineers blew open the Yellow River dikes at Huayuankou to stop a Japanese advance — deliberately flooding a vast stretch of central China, killing hundreds of thousands of Chinese civilians, and displacing millions more.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The flood the Nationalists created lasted not weeks but years: water didn't fully recede until January 1947, nearly nine years later, permanently altering the river's course across Henan province. The immediate military payoff was real but limited — the Japanese advance was slowed, not stopped. The government kept the decision secret for years and initially blamed the Japanese for the breach, one of the war's darker propaganda episodes.

events.label: The Battle of Taierzhuang
events.description: A rare major Chinese victory in 1938 punctured the myth of Japanese invincibility and lifted morale for the long war.

events.label: The Eighth Route Army
events.description: The Communist Red Army was renamed the Eighth Route Army in 1937 and nominally placed under Nationalist command — in reality it remained entirely under CCP control and used the war to build a rural political empire Japan couldn't reach.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Eighth Route Army maintained completely separate political structures, officer corps, and territorial governance from the Nationalist military it was supposedly part of. Rather than holding cities or fighting set-piece battles, it focused on organizing peasants in base areas — cutting rents, running local governments, training militias — which is how Communist Party membership grew from roughly 40,000 in 1937 to over one million by 1945. The Army was also known as the 18th Group Army, and its commanders included Zhu De and Peng Dehuai, who would both become major figures in the 1949 victory.

events.label: The Wang Jingwei Regime
events.description: The senior Nationalist Wang Jingwei defected to head a Japanese-sponsored collaborationist government in Nanjing from 1940.

events.label: The Hundred Regiments Offensive
events.description: In the summer and fall of 1940, the Eighth Route Army launched its one major conventional campaign of the war — 105 regiments attacking Japanese railways and coal mines across north China — before brutal reprisals forced a return to guerrilla tactics.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The offensive ran from August 20, 1940 to January 24, 1941 and was specifically aimed at the Shijiazhuang-Taiyuan railway, a key Japanese supply line. Japan's response was the systematic "Three Alls" (kill all, burn all, loot all) sweep through Communist base areas, which devastated the rural population the party had spent years cultivating. The lesson Mao drew from the episode — husband your strength and let the Nationalists bear the brunt — shaped Communist strategy for the rest of the war and arguably the rest of his career.

events.label: The New Fourth Army Incident
events.description: In January 1941, Nationalist forces ambushed and destroyed the headquarters column of the Communist New Fourth Army in Anhui — killing thousands of their supposed allies and ending any real cooperation between the two sides for the rest of the war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The incident is known by three names: the New Fourth Army Incident, the South Anhui Incident, and the Wannan Incident — each framing reflects whose side is telling the story. Chinese Nationalist and Communist historians still disagree on who provoked it: the ROC account holds the Communists attacked first and were being disciplined for insubordination; the PRC account calls it straightforward Nationalist treachery. After the ambush, the United Front survived only as a diplomatic fiction, with both sides essentially watching Japan and each other while waiting for the real war — the civil war — to resume.

events.label: The Bombing of Chongqing
events.description: From 1938 to 1944, Japanese aircraft conducted years of sustained air raids on Chongqing, the Nationalist wartime capital deep in the interior — one of history's first deliberate terror-bombing campaigns against a civilian city.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The bombing campaign ran officially from February 18, 1938 to December 19, 1944 — over six years — with the stated Japanese aim of breaking Chinese civilian morale and forcing the Nationalist government to surrender. It failed: Chongqing's residents adapted by building an elaborate system of tunnels and shelters into the cliffs above the Yangtze, and the government did not move again. The city's fog (it sits in a river valley notorious for low clouds) actually provided the best natural defense — many raids were cancelled or degraded because pilots couldn't find their targets.

events.label: The Burma Road and Foreign Aid
events.description: China's overland lifeline through Burma carried Allied supplies until Japan cut it in 1942, after which aid had to be flown over the Himalayas.

events.label: China Joins the Allies
events.description: Pearl Harbor pulled China into the Allied coalition in December 1941, finally ending its years of fighting Japan alone — but the American alliance came with General Joseph Stilwell, whose running feud with Chiang Kai-shek would poison US-Nationalist relations for the rest of the war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The theater was officially designated the China-Burma-India (CBI) Theater, and Stilwell held the peculiar role of simultaneously serving as US theater commander, Chiang's chief of staff, and commander of Chinese forces in Burma — three jobs that put him in conflict with almost everyone. Stilwell's nickname 'Vinegar Joe' was not ironic: he referred to Chiang in private cables as 'Peanut.' The CBI was chronically starved of Allied resources, ranking last behind Europe and the Pacific in supply priority throughout the war.

events.label: The Yan'an Rectification Movement
events.description: From 1942 to 1944, Mao ran a campaign of enforced political study, public self-criticism, and confession sessions at the Yan'an base that forged the party around his absolute leadership and invented the basic toolkit of thought-reform that would later be run on the entire country.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The movement's sharp end was run by secret-police chief Kang Sheng, who used it to extract forced confessions and destroy rivals under the guise of rooting out 'enemy agents.' At its peak, thousands of party members were under investigation or in custody. The method — correct texts, group criticism, written confession, security-apparatus enforcement — was not improvised; it drew on Soviet practices Kang had studied in Moscow in the 1930s and then adapted for Chinese conditions.

events.label: Mao Zedong Thought
events.description: At the Seventh Party Congress in April–June 1945, the CCP formally wrote 'Mao Zedong Thought' into its constitution, codifying Mao's adaptation of Marxism to Chinese peasant revolution and cementing his intellectual authority over the party.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mao Zedong Thought differed from standard Soviet Marxism-Leninism by centering the peasantry rather than the urban proletariat as the revolutionary class — a heresy in orthodox Marxist theory that Mao justified by pointing to China's overwhelming rural majority. The Seventh Congress was the first party congress held in twelve years, a gap that itself reflected how much the party had been reshaped by war and rectification. Enshrining 'Mao Zedong Thought' by name was unprecedented; no other living Communist leader had their personal ideology written into a party charter while still in power.

events.label: The Henan Famine
events.description: In 1942–43, drought combined with wartime grain requisitioning by Nationalist officials to kill an estimated two to three million people in Henan province — a catastrophe the government covered up while its armies kept taking food from starving villages.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: American journalist Theodore White broke the story for Time magazine after traveling to Henan and witnessing the famine directly, over official Nationalist protests. Peasants were reportedly eating tree bark and selling children. The famine hardened rural hostility toward Nationalist rule so thoroughly that when Japanese forces swept through Henan during Operation Ichigo in 1944, some Henan peasants disarmed retreating Nationalist soldiers rather than help them.

events.label: The Mass Line and Rent Reduction
events.description: In the base areas behind Japanese lines, the Communists applied their "mass line" approach — governing from the peasants' actual needs upward, cutting rents and debt instead of seizing land, and building a party-governed rural state that tens of millions of Chinese experienced as genuinely protective.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The mass line methodology holds that leadership should gather ideas from the people, refine them through theory, then return them to the people as policy — a cycle Mao described as "from the masses, to the masses." The deliberate moderation of the wartime policy (rent reduction, not land seizure) was a tactical choice to hold the United Front together; the same peasants who benefited from rent cuts in 1940 would become the land-reform beneficiaries of 1947. Party membership growing from 40,000 to over one million in eight years is the quantified result of this strategy working at scale.

events.label: Operation Ichigo
events.description: Japan's Operation Ichigo (April–December 1944) was the largest Japanese land offensive of the entire war — a drive through central and southern China that overran American air bases, shattered multiple Nationalist armies, and publicly exposed how badly the regime had decayed after years of war and corruption.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ichigo involved roughly 500,000 Japanese troops and covered about 1,200 miles (1,900 km) of territory, making it one of the largest single ground operations of World War II. The offensive's secondary goal was to destroy the US air bases in China from which B-29s were beginning to bomb the Japanese home islands. It succeeded militarily but came too late to change the war's outcome — the Americans shifted their Pacific bombing campaign to Mariana Islands bases instead. Communist propaganda never let the Nationalists forget that Ichigo happened while the Communists were quietly consolidating their base areas.

events.label: The Cairo Conference
events.description: In November 1943, Chiang Kai-shek met Roosevelt and Churchill in Cairo — the first time China had sat at the table with Western powers as an equal — and walked away with promises of territorial restoration and a permanent seat on the future UN Security Council.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Cairo Declaration committed the Allies to stripping Japan of all territories seized since 1914 and returning Manchuria, Taiwan, and the Pescadores (Penghu Islands) to China. It was one of the first times any Allied conference explicitly addressed the postwar map of Asia. Churchill privately considered China a 'faggot vote' (a proxy bloc) and resented its elevation to great-power status; he was outvoted by Roosevelt, who wanted a strong China as a postwar partner in Asia.

events.label: The Dixie Mission
events.description: In July 1944, a team of US Army officers and diplomats flew to the Communist headquarters at Yan'an — the first official American contact with the CCP — and sent back reports that the Communists were disciplined, popular, and competent in ways the Nationalists had stopped being.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The mission was codenamed 'Dixie' as a wry joke: 'Dixie' because they were going to the territory of the rebels. It ran for nearly three years, from July 1944 to March 1947. The glowing reports from officers like John Service and John Davies contributed to the later 'Who Lost China' political firestorm in Washington, with the diplomats accused of pro-Communist sympathy and hounded out of the State Department during the McCarthy era.

events.label: Japan's Surrender
events.description: Japan surrendered in August 1945 following the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and a Soviet invasion of Manchuria that destroyed Japan's million-man Kwantung Army in a single week — leaving a strategic vacuum in China's industrial north that Communist forces rushed to fill.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Soviet Union declared war on Japan on August 8, 1945 — exactly three months after Germany's defeat, as Stalin had promised at Yalta. The Soviets deliberately delayed handing Manchuria's Japanese-seized arsenals and heavy industry over to the Nationalists, giving Communist forces time to move in and inherit them. Emperor Hirohito's surrender announcement on August 15 caught both Chinese sides by surprise; the Nationalist government was based in Chongqing, 1,500 miles (2,400 km) from the key Manchurian cities it now had to race to occupy.

events.label: Wartime Hyperinflation
events.description: Cut off from coastal customs revenue, the Nationalist government funded the war by printing money — triggering a hyperinflation that ran from the early 1940s through 1949 and wiped out the savings and salaries of the urban middle class the regime depended on.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: By the late 1940s inflation was running at thousands of percent annually; the government issued ever-larger denomination notes until a gold yuan currency reform in 1948 tried and failed to stabilize things. Professors, civil servants, and army officers saw their real incomes collapse to near zero, making graft the only rational survival strategy — a dynamic that turned corruption from a personal failing into a structural feature of the state. The inflation is widely credited by historians as doing more damage to Nationalist legitimacy in the cities than any military defeat.

events.label: The Chongqing Negotiations
events.description: In August 1945, Mao flew to the Nationalist stronghold of Chongqing for six weeks of US-brokered talks with Chiang Kai-shek — his first time in Nationalist-held territory in nearly two decades. Both sides signed the Double Tenth Agreement on October 10, 1945, and neither side ever intended to honor it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The talks lasted exactly 43 days and concluded on October 10 — Double Ten Day, the anniversary of the 1911 revolution that had ended the Qing dynasty, lending the signing a symbolic weight that made its rapid collapse all the more pointed. Mao's decision to fly to Chongqing was a personal gamble: he was putting himself inside enemy territory at a moment when both sides' armies were racing to seize Japanese-surrendered positions. The agreement called for a political consultative conference and a unified national army — the two things neither party would ever actually allow.

events.label: The Marshall Mission
events.description: General George Marshall — America's most celebrated soldier and future architect of the Marshall Plan for Europe — spent all of 1946 in China trying to broker a coalition government between the Communists and Nationalists. He failed, and the mission's collapse marked Washington's effective withdrawal from the mediator role.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The photograph of Zhang Zhizhong, Marshall, and Zhou Enlai together captures the central absurdity of the mission: two Leninist party-armies were being asked to voluntarily merge into a single neutral national force, which would mean each party surrendering the instrument of its own survival. Marshall later said it was the most frustrating assignment of his career. When he left in January 1947, he publicly blamed both sides — an unusually candid rebuke from a diplomat of his stature.

events.label: The Civil War Resumes
events.description: Full-scale civil war between the Nationalists and Communists resumed in 1946, picking up a conflict that had been running, with a wartime pause, since 1927. The Nationalists held the cities, railways, and American equipment; the Communists held the countryside and a peasant army that moved freely between the garrison points.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The armed conflict ran from August 1, 1927 all the way to December 10, 1949 — over 22 years in total, making it one of the longest civil wars of the twentieth century. In 1946 most outside observers, including Stalin, expected the Nationalists to win: they outnumbered Communist forces and had US equipment. The strategic trap they fell into was classic guerrilla mathematics — garrisoning cities and rail lines required so many troops that the space between the cities was effectively conceded to the enemy.

events.label: The Outline Land Law
events.description: In 1947 the Communist Party abandoned its moderate wartime rent-reduction policy and ordered radical land redistribution across the territory it controlled: landlords' land was seized and handed to poor peasants, turning the rural majority into the PLA's most committed recruits and supply base.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The campaign — known in Chinese as Tugai (土改) — redistributed land to hundreds of millions of peasants who had never owned any. Landlords were subjected to public 'struggle sessions' in which former tenants denounced, beat, and in many cases killed them; death toll estimates range from hundreds of thousands to millions. As a war strategy it was devastatingly effective: a peasant who had just received a landlord's field had an existential personal stake in a Communist victory, and often a son already in the People's Liberation Army.

events.label: The Liaoshen Campaign
events.description: The Liaoshen Campaign (September–November 1948) was the first of three massive Communist offensives that ended the civil war. Lin Biao's forces destroyed the Nationalists' best remaining armies across Manchuria in 52 days, capturing Jinzhou, Changchun, and Shenyang and giving the Communists a numerical advantage over the Nationalists for the first time.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before Liaoshen, the Nationalists had more troops, better equipment, and American backing — on paper they looked like the likely winners. The campaign's decisive moment was the fall of Jinzhou, which cut off Nationalist forces in Manchuria from retreat by sea; once isolated, the northern cities fell in sequence. The 52-day campaign ended with the Communists capturing the whole of Manchuria, a vast industrial and agricultural base that had been Japan's main conquest a decade earlier.

events.label: The Huaihai Campaign
events.description: The Huaihai Campaign (November 1948 – January 1949) was the largest battle of the civil war — over a million men on each side fighting across the central China plains. It annihilated the Nationalist armies between the Yellow River and the Yangtze and opened the road south, decided as much by millions of peasant civilians pushing supply wheelbarrows for the PLA as by the fighting itself.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The campaign began on November 6, 1948 with a PLA offensive against the Nationalist headquarters at Xuzhou, and ended on January 10, 1949 when PLA forces reached the north bank of the Yangtze. The logistics story is extraordinary: the PLA's supply chain across the central plains depended almost entirely on civilian labor — millions of peasants, many of them recent land-reform beneficiaries, moving ammunition, food, and wounded on foot and by wheelbarrow. It is sometimes called the battle that civilians won.

events.label: The Pingjin Campaign
events.description: The Pingjin Campaign (November 1948 – January 1949) cleared northern China: Tianjin was taken by storm and Beijing surrendered by negotiation, sparing the ancient capital from bombardment. With the north lost, the Nationalist position in China was irretrievably gone.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Pingjin ('Ping' for Beiping, the old name for Beijing; 'Jin' for Tianjin) lasted 64 days and ended on January 31, 1949. The negotiated surrender of Beijing was a deliberate Communist choice — Mao wanted the symbolic capital intact, and the Nationalist commander Fu Zuoyi agreed to terms that allowed his troops to be absorbed rather than destroyed. The campaign concluded Nationalist dominance across the entire North China Plain in a single winter offensive.

events.label: The Gold Yuan Collapse
events.description: In August 1948 the Nationalist government replaced its collapsing currency with the 'gold yuan,' forcing citizens to hand over their gold, silver, and foreign currency in exchange — then hyperinflated the new currency into worthlessness within months, wiping out the urban middle class that had been the regime's core support.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The legal exchange rate was set at 0.22217 grams of gold per gold yuan — a rate the government could not honor from day one. Citizens were compelled by executive order to convert their savings at a rate of one gold yuan to three million of the old fabi yuan. The economic wipeout was so complete and so fast that it destroyed the ROC government's most important urban constituency; historians consider it one of the primary reasons the Nationalist state collapsed so quickly in 1949.

events.label: Crossing the Yangtze
events.description: On the night of April 20, 1949, the People's Liberation Army crossed the Yangtze River — the great geographic barrier dividing north and south China — and took the Nationalist capital Nanjing within days, ending organized Nationalist resistance on the mainland.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Yangtze crossing campaign ran from April 20 to June 2, 1949, concluding with the fall of both Nanjing and Shanghai — China's financial capital — to Communist forces. The PLA occupied the presidential palace in Nanjing and photographed themselves there; the image (File:People's_Liberation_Army_occupied_the_presidential_palace_1949.jpg) became an iconic symbol of the revolution's completeness. The Nationalist government had already begun transferring its gold reserves, treasuries, and the imperial art collection to Taiwan before the crossing.

events.label: The Retreat to Taiwan
events.description: Beginning in December 1949, Chiang Kai-shek's government retreated to Taiwan — taking roughly two million soldiers, officials, and civilians, the national gold reserve, and a massive trove of imperial art from the Forbidden City. The civil war did not end; it simply froze across the Taiwan Strait, and technically remains frozen today.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The retreat is called the 'Great Retreat' (大撤退) in Taiwan. The art collection transferred to Taiwan — over 690,000 objects from the National Palace collection — now forms the core of the National Palace Museum in Taipei, one of the world's great repositories of Chinese art. Taiwan had only been returned from 50 years of Japanese rule in 1945; Chiang's government was its third foreign administration in a generation, after the Qing and Japan.

events.label: New Democracy and the United Front
events.description: The 1949 political consultative conference let minor parties and non-Communists co-found the new state under firm party control.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The idea came from Mao's 1940 essay "On New Democracy," which argued that China was not ready for socialism and would pass through a coalition stage, led by the Communists but including the "national bourgeoisie" and the minor parties. The 1949 conference gave the theory a stage set: the small "democratic parties" got seats, a flag and an anthem were chosen, and a Common Program stood in for a constitution. The united front was genuine enough to reassure businessmen and intellectuals, and brief enough that within a few years those same parties were ornamental and private enterprise was being absorbed by the state.

events.label: The Common Program
events.description: The Common Program was China's provisional constitution from 1949 to 1954, passed by the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference the same month the PRC was proclaimed — a founding document that promised a moderate, multi-class "New Democracy" before the full socialist turn.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The program was adopted at the very first plenary session of the CPPCC in September 1949, just weeks before Mao's October 1 proclamation from Tiananmen. It served as the supreme law of the new state for five years until the PRC's first formal constitution was ratified in 1954. Minor non-Communist parties were given seats under its framework, a coalition facade that gave the new government a broader-than-party face to both domestic skeptics and foreign observers.

events.label: The Sino-Soviet Treaty
events.description: Mao spent two months in Moscow to secure a 1950 alliance and loans from Stalin, anchoring China in the Soviet bloc.

events.label: The Marriage Law of 1950
events.description: The Marriage Law of 1950 banned arranged marriage, child betrothal, concubinage, and the sale of women, and gave women the right to divorce and to own property — directly dismantling the Confucian patriarchal family structure that two thousand years of Chinese law had upheld.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Millions of women exercised the divorce provision almost immediately, often over fierce resistance from husbands and in-laws; the backlash included violence and a documented wave of suicides by women denied divorces. The New Culture Movement intellectuals of the 1910s–1920s had attacked the same patriarchal system with essays and manifestos, but no Chinese government before 1950 had translated that critique into enforceable law. Enforcement was uneven and later subordinated to political campaigns, but the legal framework of female subordination — the statutory right to sell, betroth, or confine women — was gone.

events.label: Suppression of Counterrevolutionaries
events.description: The Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries, launched in March 1950, targeted former Nationalist officials, alleged bandits, and anyone branded an enemy of the new order — executing hundreds of thousands and running until 1953.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The campaign was formally initiated by a Central Committee directive specifically ordering the elimination of bandits and the establishment of a "revolutionary new order" — it was not ad hoc but a planned instrument of state consolidation. The banner of the Korean War's "Resist America, Aid Korea" mobilization was used to justify the crackdown at home: wartime patriotism made questioning the executions politically dangerous. The campaign was one of several running simultaneously — alongside land reform and the Three-Anti/Five-Anti drives — that together killed more people in three years of peace than many wars.

events.label: The Three-Anti and Five-Anti Campaigns
events.description: The Three-Anti Campaign (1951, targeting corruption within the Party and state) and Five-Anti Campaign (1952, targeting urban capitalists) together broke what remained of China's private business class and consolidated the CCP's control over city economies.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The "three antis" were corruption, waste, and bureaucratism — notionally a Party self-cleaning exercise. The "five antis" targeted bribery, tax evasion, theft of state property, cheating on government contracts, and stealing economic information — charges that could be leveled at almost any private businessman who had operated under the pre-1949 system. The campaigns consolidated Mao's power by removing capitalists who might have anchored any future pluralist alternative, and they effectively ended the "New Democracy" mixed-economy promise of the Common Program years ahead of formal collectivization.
