events.label: The Annexation of Tibet
events.description: The Seventeen Point Agreement of May 1951 formalized the PLA's incorporation of Tibet into the PRC — signed under military occupation by Tibetan representatives, it is remembered as liberation by Beijing and as annexation under duress by the Tibetan exile government and most outside historians.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The US government actively lobbied the 14th Dalai Lama to denounce the agreement and flee Tibet before he ratified it, reasoning that a public disavowal would give Washington stronger grounds to condemn Chinese aggression — the Dalai Lama instead ratified via telegraph in October 1951. The agreement did preserve the Tibetan local government and the Dalai Lama's authority on paper; those provisions collapsed in the 1959 uprising (Chapter 12). The agreement was signed in Zhongnanhai, the leadership compound in Beijing, by Tibetan plenipotentiaries who had traveled there after the PLA's military entry.

events.label: The Incorporation of Xinjiang
events.description: In 1949 the PLA entered Xinjiang (the vast, predominantly Muslim far northwest, roughly one-sixth of China's land area), ending the semi-independent East Turkestan Republic and beginning the long process of Han settlement and military colonization of the region.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Xinjiang had been only loosely controlled by the late Qing dynasty and was effectively autonomous from Beijing after 1912; by 1944 an armed revolt had established the short-lived East Turkestan Republic in the north, backed by the Soviet Union. The Soviet-backed ETR leadership died in a plane crash en route to Beijing for negotiations in August 1949, weeks before the PRC's proclamation — removing the main alternative power center right as the PLA moved in. The Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps (Bingtuan), a paramilitary farming and settlement organization, was established in 1954 and became the instrument of long-term demographic transformation.

events.label: Thought Reform of Intellectuals
events.description: Universities and professionals were put through study, confession, and self-criticism to remold the old educated class.

events.label: Resist America, Aid Korea
events.description: "Resist America, Aid Korea" was the mass domestic mobilization campaign that ran alongside the Korean War (1950–53), harnessing wartime patriotism to rally the population, raise funds, and justify a sweeping crackdown on anyone branded a domestic enemy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The campaign fused anti-American sentiment with loyalty to the new state in ways that proved durable for decades — it was the moment the PRC established its foundational narrative of standing up to Western imperialism. Ordinary citizens were organized to donate jewelry, savings, and grain to the war effort; schools and factories held pledge rallies. At home, the campaign's banner covered the simultaneously running Campaign to Suppress Counterrevolutionaries and the Three-Anti/Five-Anti drives, making opposition to any of them look like treasonous sympathy for the enemy.

events.label: The First Five-Year Plan
events.description: China's First Five-Year Plan (1953–1957) channeled Soviet loans and expertise into heavy industry — steel, machine tools, power plants — building an industrial base almost from scratch in five years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The plan was modeled directly on Stalin's Soviet industrialization drives of the 1930s, prioritizing producer goods over consumer goods. Chinese central planners, many trained in Moscow, had to learn from scratch how to run a command economy at continental scale. Growth in industrial output during the plan period was genuinely impressive, giving the CCP leadership (including Mao) a false confidence that even more radical acceleration could work — a key mental precondition for the Great Leap.

events.label: The Soviet 156 Projects
events.description: A package of roughly 156 large Soviet-designed industrial projects — steel mills, power stations, vehicle factories — gave the People's Republic its first modern industrial infrastructure and trained the engineers who would run it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The projects were spread across inland cities like Wuhan, Xi'an, and Chengdu rather than coastal ports, partly for defense reasons and partly to reduce regional inequality. Soviet engineers lived on-site and ran hands-on training programs; tens of thousands of Chinese technicians were sent to the USSR for advanced study. When Soviet advisers abruptly pulled out in 1960, they took their blueprints with them — deliberately leaving some projects mid-construction as a lever in the political dispute.

events.label: Agricultural Collectivization
events.description: Between 1953 and 1956 China's peasants — who had just received their own land in the land reform — were moved through mutual-aid teams into full collective farms, where private plots were pooled and households no longer farmed independently.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: By the end of 1956 over 90 percent of peasant households had been incorporated into higher-level cooperatives (essentially collective farms), a pace that stunned even Soviet advisers. Mao personally overrode more cautious colleagues in a 1955 speech calling for a "high tide" of collectivization, dismissing the evidence of peasant resistance and grain shortfalls. The result was that Chinese peasants experienced the full arc — private land, expropriation under landlords, land back in land reform, land pooled again in collectives — all within roughly a decade.

events.label: The 1954 Constitution
events.description: China's first PRC constitution, adopted in September 1954, created the National People's Congress as the formal legislature and laid out a state structure — while leaving real power firmly with the Communist Party.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The constitution was modeled closely on the 1936 Soviet constitution (sometimes called the "Stalin Constitution"), right down to its enumeration of rights that existed only on paper. Mao Zedong was elected the first Chairman of the People's Republic under it, combining the top party and state roles. The constitution was effectively suspended during the Cultural Revolution and replaced entirely in 1975 with a much shorter document that explicitly named the party's leading role.

events.label: The Gao Gang Affair
events.description: Gao Gang, the powerful boss of Manchuria, and Rao Shushi, who ran eastern China, were accused in 1953–54 of trying to split the party and build independent power bases — the first major purge inside the new state's leadership.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gao Gang controlled Manchuria, the industrial heartland the Soviets had stripped and then rebuilt, and had cultivated a direct personal relationship with Stalin that bypassed Beijing — a dangerous independent resource. After his case was raised at party meetings, he killed himself in August 1954 before formal sentencing, which was almost unprecedented at the CCP leadership level. Rao Shushi was imprisoned and died in custody in 1975, having never been rehabilitated.

events.label: The Socialist Transformation of Industry
events.description: In 1955–56 the state absorbed nearly all remaining private businesses into joint state-private enterprises, completing the "Three Great Transformations" — of agriculture, handicrafts, and industry — and ending the mixed economy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The transformation of industry and commerce was striking for its speed: whereas the Soviet NEP mixed economy lasted years before being crushed, China's equivalent lasted only a few years before being swept away. Former private owners were kept on as salaried managers and paid a fixed annual return on their assets (called "fixed interest"), a formula designed to prevent capital flight and maintain technical continuity. Fixed interest payments continued until 1966, when the Cultural Revolution ended even that vestigial arrangement.

events.label: Pinyin and the Common Speech
events.description: Pinyin — a Roman-alphabet system for spelling out Mandarin pronunciation — was developed in the mid-1950s and officially adopted in 1958 to help teach standard spoken Chinese and accelerate mass literacy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Pinyin replaced a thicket of competing romanization systems, the most widely used being the older Wade-Giles scheme (which rendered Mao's name as "Mao Tse-tung" and Beijing as "Peking"). Its inventor, linguist Zhou Youguang, worked on it while employed as a banker in Shanghai and finished the core system in just three years; he lived to 111 and spent his later decades as a critic of the party. The UN adopted pinyin as the standard romanization for Chinese in 1982, which is why this book spells everything the way it does.

events.label: The De-Stalinization Shock
events.description: Khrushchev's secret 1956 speech denouncing Stalin's cult of personality rattled the Communist world — and pushed Mao to write his own answer, a speech called "On the Ten Major Relationships," staking out a distinctively Chinese path.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Khrushchev's speech was delivered to a closed session but leaked within weeks and caused near-panic in Communist parties worldwide, including Hungary (where it helped spark a revolution that the Soviets crushed). Mao's "Ten Major Relationships" response, delivered in April 1956, argued China should learn from Soviet mistakes by balancing heavy and light industry, and coastal versus inland development — but it also implicitly claimed Mao had avoided Stalin's errors, a confidence the next decade would test badly. The speech was not published in China until 1976, after Mao's death.

events.label: The Anti-Rightist Campaign
events.description: The Anti-Rightist Campaign (1957–59) reversed the Hundred Flowers opening: roughly 550,000 people who had spoken up were labeled "rightists" and sent to labor camps or internal exile, silencing China's intellectual class for twenty years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: "Rightist" was a political label, not an ideological description — many targets were loyal Communists who had merely taken Mao's invitation to criticize seriously. Deng Xiaoping ran the campaign's implementation as party general secretary, a role that came back to haunt his reputation when he himself was purged in the Cultural Revolution. Rightists were formally rehabilitated only in 1978–79 under Deng's own post-Mao government, though the rehabilitation documents often stated they had been "wrongly labeled" rather than admitting the campaign itself was wrong.

events.label: The People's Communes
events.description: Starting in 1958, China's villages were merged into massive People's Communes — units of tens of thousands of households that pooled land, tools, labor, and even cooking, replacing private kitchens with communal mess halls and abolishing the private plots peasants had relied on.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At their peak, roughly 26,000 communes covered nearly all of rural China, each functioning more like a military unit than a village — members were organized into brigades and work teams and could be deployed anywhere the state needed labor. The brief period when mess halls offered unlimited free food was remembered decades later by survivors as the moment many families ate through their entire grain reserves before the famine set in.

events.label: The Backyard Furnaces
events.description: To hit state-ordered steel production quotas, hundreds of thousands of crude clay-and-brick furnaces were built in villages across China — fueled by whatever wood was available and fed with peasants' own pots, tools, and door hinges — producing metal so brittle and impure it was almost entirely unusable.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The steel campaign pulled tens of millions of agricultural workers off the autumn 1958 harvest at exactly the wrong moment, leaving crops to rot unharvested in the fields. Local officials who failed to meet steel quotas faced punishment as class enemies, so the furnaces kept burning even as it became obvious the output was worthless. An estimated 90% or more of the backyard steel was too low-quality to use in any industrial process.

events.label: The Sputnik Fields
events.description: Local officials across China reported fantastically inflated grain harvests — so-called 'sputnik fields' supposedly producing ten or a hundred times the real yield — and the state then set procurement quotas against those fake numbers, physically removing nearly all the actual grain and leaving villages to starve.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The most stricken provinces were Anhui (where roughly 18% of the population died), Chongqing (15%), Sichuan (13%), Guizhou (11%), and Hunan (8%). Peasants caught attempting to flee famine zones or even to report the starvation could be accused of 'right deviation' — a political crime that carried its own lethal consequences. The procurement system continued extracting grain for urban centers and Soviet-machinery exports even as famine deaths accelerated in the countryside.

events.label: The Four Pests Campaign
events.description: The Four Pests Campaign mobilized hundreds of millions of people to eradicate rats, flies, mosquitoes, and sparrows — but wiping out sparrows removed a natural check on locusts and other crop-eating insects, which then exploded in population and devastated the very harvests the campaign was meant to protect.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The sparrow-killing drive was strikingly total: citizens banged drums and pots continuously to keep birds airborne until they dropped from exhaustion, and schoolchildren competed to collect dead sparrows. Ornithologist Zheng Zuoxin warned publicly in 1959 that eliminating sparrows would trigger insect explosions, and was subsequently branded a rightist. The campaign was quietly revised in 1960, replacing sparrows with bedbugs as the fourth target — by which point the ecological damage was done.

events.label: The Lushan Conference
events.description: At a 1959 Communist Party leadership summit at the mountain resort of Lushan, Defense Minister Peng Dehuai privately handed Mao a letter describing the real damage the Great Leap was causing — and Mao responded by publicly destroying him, purging him and all who agreed, and ensuring no official anywhere in China dared report the famine for two more years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Peng's letter was relatively cautious — he praised the Leap's goals while noting practical problems — but Mao circulated it to the full Politburo as a political attack and demanded everyone choose sides. The conference ran July–August 1959, immediately followed by a nationwide 'anti-right opportunism' campaign that purged an estimated 3.6 million officials who had expressed similar doubts. After Lushan, grain procurement actually intensified against a collapsing harvest, and the death toll that might have peaked in 1959 instead ground forward for two more years.

events.label: The Second Taiwan Strait Crisis
events.description: Heavy shelling of the Nationalist-held islands of Quemoy in 1958 brought China and the US close to nuclear confrontation.

events.label: The 1959 Tibetan Uprising
events.description: A failed Lhasa revolt in 1959 ended Tibetan autonomy and sent the Dalai Lama into permanent exile in India.

events.label: Mao Steps Back
events.description: Mao gave up the state chairmanship to Liu Shaoqi in 1959, a handover that set up the later clash over the famine and reform.

events.label: The Great Chinese Famine
events.description: The Great Leap Forward's catastrophic grain policies triggered history's deadliest famine between 1959 and 1961, with scholarly estimates of excess deaths ranging from 15 million to 45 million — a man-made disaster the regime concealed for years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The most stricken provinces were Anhui, where an estimated 18% of the population died, and Sichuan at 13% — meaning roughly one in six or seven people in those provinces perished. The Chinese journalist Yang Jisheng, who had privileged access to party archives, spent nearly two decades gathering evidence for his book *Tombstone*, naming the famine after the tombstone he erected for his own father who had starved to death during it.

events.label: The Xinyang Incident
events.description: In China's Xinyang prefecture (Henan province), roughly a million people starved in 1959–60 while local granaries held grain throughout — local officials refused to release food or report the famine because admitting failure would have destroyed their political careers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Xinyang was one of the first regions to achieve 100% collectivization and its party leaders had championed the Leap loudest, making the famine impossible to acknowledge without career-ending self-indictment. Peasants were forbidden to leave in search of food; those who tried were turned back at checkpoints — making it not a food shortage but an enforced starvation.

events.label: The Seven Thousand Cadres Conference
events.description: In January–February 1962, over 7,000 Communist Party officials gathered in Beijing for the largest work conference in party history, where Liu Shaoqi publicly declared the famine was "three parts natural, seven parts man-made" — directly contradicting Mao's narrative to his face.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mao made a formal self-criticism at the conference — one of the very few times he ever did so — but gave no ground on ideology, describing his errors as those of a "pioneer" rather than a failed leader. After the conference Mao retreated into a semi-retired role, later describing Liu and Deng as having "pushed him aside like a dead ancestor" — a resentment he nursed until the Cultural Revolution.

events.label: The Liu-Deng Recovery
events.description: After the famine's peak, Liu Shaoqi (head of state) and Deng Xiaoping (party general secretary) dismantled the most destructive Great Leap policies — disbanding communal kitchens, restoring household farming plots, and reviving rural markets — pulling the economy out of collapse by 1962.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Liu had joined the Communist Party in 1921 in Shanghai and was one of its founding generation — his pragmatism wasn't ideological defection but practical survival instinct built over four decades. His success in the recovery is precisely what made him Mao's primary target in the Cultural Revolution; Mao ultimately had him expelled from the party in 1968, and Liu died in prison in 1969, denied medical treatment.

events.label: The Soviet Advisors Withdraw
events.description: In July 1960, Moscow abruptly recalled all 1,400 Soviet technical advisers from China and withdrew the blueprints for hundreds of ongoing industrial and infrastructure projects — leaving factories half-built and nuclear programs stalled at the worst possible moment, mid-famine.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The advisers' withdrawal halted 156 major Soviet-aided industrial projects, from steel plants to aircraft factories, many of which sat unfinished for years. The move confirmed Mao's long-held suspicion that reliance on any outside power was a strategic trap — accelerating his push for complete self-reliance ("self-strengthening"), the same logic that had driven the disastrous Great Leap Forward in the first place.

events.label: The Sino-Indian War
events.description: China and India fought a short, sharp border war in October–November 1962 in the high Himalayas, with Chinese forces routing Indian troops and seizing disputed frontier territory — a humiliation for India that still shapes the two countries' relationship.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The war was fought along two completely separate fronts: the Aksai Chin plateau in the west (claimed by both but already held by China, which had secretly built a road through it in the 1950s) and the North-East Frontier Agency (today Arunachal Pradesh) in the east. China declared a unilateral ceasefire and withdrew to pre-war positions after its decisive military victory — which analysts interpreted as a calculated demonstration of power rather than a territorial grab, since China kept Aksai Chin but gave back the eastern gains.

events.label: The Socialist Education Movement
events.description: Between 1963 and 1965, Mao launched the Socialist Education Movement (also called the Four Cleanups) to purge "capitalist" and "corrupt" elements from rural party branches — officially a cleanup campaign, but really Mao's first test of using political mobilization to attack the party apparatus he now distrusted.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The movement's four targets were corruption in "politics, economics, organization, and ideology" — an intentionally vague mandate that allowed Mao to direct it wherever he chose. By 1964 it was producing tens of thousands of investigations and purges; Liu Shaoqi tried to redirect it into a more orderly process with party oversight, a jurisdictional fight that revealed the exact fault line Mao would explode with the Cultural Revolution two years later.

events.label: Learn from Dazhai
events.description: Mao held up the model brigade Dazhai and the Daqing oilfield as proof that self-reliant socialist zeal could replace expertise and aid.

events.label: The Dismissal of Hai Rui
events.description: The historical play *Hai Rui Dismissed from Office*, written by Beijing deputy mayor Wu Han in 1961, depicted a loyal Ming-dynasty official unjustly fired by the emperor — and was widely understood within the party as a coded defense of Peng Dehuai, the general Mao had purged for telling the truth about the Great Leap.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hai Rui was a real 16th-century Ming official celebrated for honesty and the defense of peasants; Wu Han had written admiringly of him in 1959, just as Peng Dehuai was being purged, and the parallel was not subtle. The play ran unmolested for four years until November 1965, when Mao's wife Jiang Qing commissioned a denunciation piece published in Shanghai — the opening shot of the Cultural Revolution, deliberately fired outside Beijing where Liu and Deng held sway.

events.label: Learn from Lei Feng
events.description: The cult of a selfless model soldier, promoted by Lin Biao from 1963, primed the population for total devotion to Mao.

events.label: Lin Biao and the Mao Cult
events.description: Defense Minister Lin Biao systematically converted the People's Liberation Army into a vehicle for Mao worship, producing the Little Red Book and rising to be named Mao's successor — a position that would prove fatal.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Lin Biao suffered from severe hypochondria and phobias, including documented fears of water, wind, and light, which increasingly limited his public appearances. Despite commanding some of the most decisive campaigns of the Civil War, he was far more comfortable as an ideological operator than a functioning minister. The 1969 party constitution was the only time in CCP history that a designated successor was written into the party charter by name.

events.label: The May 16 Circular
events.description: Mao's May 1966 secret directive declared the Communist Party itself had been infiltrated by counter-revolutionaries, dissolved the existing cultural apparatus, and set the Cultural Revolution formally in motion.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Circular was kept secret from the broader public for a full year — it was only published in the People's Daily on May 17, 1967, after the movement was already in full destructive swing. It grew out of a political dispute over a single Beijing Opera play, Hai Rui Dismissed from Office, which Mao's allies argued was an allegory defending the disgraced official Peng Dehuai. The Cultural Revolution Group established by the Circular bypassed the entire normal party structure and reported directly to Mao.

events.label: The Big-Character Posters
events.description: Handwritten wall posters covered in large accusatory text became the Cultural Revolution's defining medium — anyone could denounce anyone, and the first famous poster targeting party officials appeared at Peking University in May 1966.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The very first big-character poster of the Cultural Revolution was written by a philosophy lecturer named Nie Yuanzi, targeting Peking University's own administration; Mao praised it as 'the first Marxist-Leninist big-character poster in the country.' At their peak in 1966–67, millions of posters plastered city walls nationwide, and their authors sometimes gained overnight political power or faced immediate mortal danger depending on whether their targets survived. Mao himself used big-character posters — he wrote one titled 'Bombard the Headquarters' in August 1966 to signal his backing of the radical faction over the party establishment.

events.label: The Tiananmen Rallies
events.description: Between August and November 1966, Mao held eight mass rallies at Tiananmen Square, reviewing an estimated 11 million Red Guards from across the country and giving the movement his personal blessing.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The rallies began at dawn and lasted all day; Red Guards traveled for free on trains and were housed in schools and military barracks in Beijing — the government essentially mobilized the national rail network to move millions of young people to the capital. Mao typically appeared on the Tiananmen gate-tower in military uniform, waving at the crowds below, and the sight of him caused many Red Guards to weep. The sheer logistical undertaking — feeding and moving millions in 1966 China — was itself a feat, though it also stretched the country's infrastructure to breaking point.

events.label: The Fall of Liu Shaoqi
events.description: Liu Shaoqi, the head of state of the People's Republic and the man who had told the truth about the Great Leap famine, was denounced as the 'number one capitalist roader,' stripped of all offices, subjected to brutal struggle sessions, and left to die untreated in a prison cellar in November 1969.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Liu died of diabetes complications after his medication was deliberately withheld; by the end, guards reportedly didn't recognize him because he was so emaciated. His death was kept secret from the public for nearly a decade — it was not officially acknowledged until 1980, when he was posthumously rehabilitated and declared 'a great Marxist.' His wife Wang Guangmei was forced to wear a necklace of ping-pong balls at her own struggle session — a mockery of pearls she had worn on a state visit — in front of crowds of tens of thousands.

events.label: The Wuhan Incident
events.description: In July 1967 a military-backed mass organization in Wuhan seized central government envoys sent to resolve factional fighting, triggering a standoff that nearly turned the Cultural Revolution into full-scale civil war between the army and the radical center.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The central emissaries seized were Wang Li and Xie Fuzhi, two of the most powerful members of the Cultural Revolution Group; their detention for several days by the local military commander Chen Zaidao was unprecedented defiance of Mao's inner circle. Gunboats appeared on the Yangtze River and airborne troops were reportedly placed on alert. The incident forced Mao to intervene personally, and paradoxically it accelerated the drive to arm civilian Red Guard factions — leading to even worse factional fighting nationwide in late 1967.

events.label: Down to the Countryside
events.description: From 1968 the Down to the Countryside Movement forcibly sent roughly 17 million urban young people — mostly Red Guards — to remote rural villages, dispersing the movement and creating a 'lost generation' denied education and career for years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Most sent-down youth spent between two and ten years in villages with no clear path home; many were stranded until Mao's death and the end of the Cultural Revolution in 1976. A young Xi Jinping was sent to a poor cave-dwelling village in Shaanxi province at age 15, where he spent seven years — an experience he has repeatedly cited as formative. Conditions were often harsh: some youth faced brutal rural poverty, sexual violence, and were forbidden from returning even when parents died.

events.label: Cleansing the Class Ranks
events.description: The Cleansing the Class Ranks campaign of 1968–69 was the Cultural Revolution's deadliest and least-remembered phase — a systematic bureaucratic purge run through work units that killed on the order of a million people with little of the street-level drama of the Red Guard years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Unlike the chaotic Red Guard phase, this campaign was organized and methodical: every work unit, factory, school, and army unit was required to identify 'hidden enemies' within its own ranks, making it nearly impossible to escape by staying quiet. Historians estimate it was responsible for more deaths than the entire Red Guard period precisely because it was systematic and state-directed rather than mob-driven. Many victims were accused of being members of the '516 Elements' — an alleged secret radical faction — a charge so vague it could be applied to almost anyone.

events.label: The Ninth Party Congress
events.description: The April 1969 Ninth Party Congress declared the Cultural Revolution's first phase a triumph, installed a militarized new party leadership, and wrote Lin Biao into the constitution by name as Mao's designated successor.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The 1,512 delegates were dominated by military officers — a marked shift from the civilian party of the 1950s. The congress formally expelled Liu Shaoqi from the party and erased Deng Xiaoping's name from official records. Writing a successor's name into the party constitution was constitutionally unprecedented in CCP history, and within two years Mao would be moving to destroy the very man he had just elevated.

events.label: The Shanghai January Storm
events.description: Radicals seized the Shanghai government in early 1967; the experiment was reined into army-led 'revolutionary committees'.

events.label: The Zhenbao Island Clash
events.description: A seven-month undeclared border war between China and the Soviet Union in 1969 — two nuclear-armed Communist powers nearly going to full-scale war with each other — that shattered any pretense of socialist solidarity and pushed China to find a new strategic patron.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The most intense fighting happened at Damansky/Zhenbao Island, a tiny sandbar on the Ussuri River that marked the disputed border — an absurdly small piece of ground that triggered a nuclear scare. The Soviets, rattled enough to seriously consider a pre-emptive strike on China's nuclear facilities, sent unofficial feelers to Washington asking how the US might react. That inquiry helped convince American strategists that the Sino-Soviet split was real and deep enough to exploit.

events.label: The Lin Biao Incident
events.description: Lin Biao — Mao's constitutionally designated successor and the man who had compiled the Little Red Book — died in a plane crash over Mongolia in September 1971, supposedly fleeing to the Soviet Union after a failed coup attempt, in an event so murky that serious historians still dispute the basic facts.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Lin had been a genuine military hero: he commanded the Manchurian Field Army that swept Nationalist forces out of Northeast China in the civil war and was ranked third among the ten founding marshals of the PRC. His name had literally been written into the 1969 constitution as Mao's successor — making his posthumous denunciation as a traitor an unacknowledged admission that the Party's own founding document had been wrong. The official story (coup plot, defection, crash) has never been independently verified; some historians suspect Lin was already dead before the plane took off.

events.label: Ping-Pong Diplomacy
events.description: In April 1971 an American table-tennis player named Glenn Cowan accidentally boarded the Chinese team's bus at the World Championships in Nagoya, Japan, and the resulting friendly encounter with star player Zhuang Zedong sparked an invitation that became the first cultural exchange between the US and China in over two decades.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The encounter between Cowan and Zhuang was genuinely accidental — Cowan missed his own team's bus — but Chinese officials had to decide in minutes whether to let Zhuang be photographed with an American, effectively asking Mao's permission at the highest level. Mao approved, the US team was invited to China, and Kissinger later cited ping-pong diplomacy as the perfect opening gesture precisely because it was people-to-people and deniable: no government had officially committed to anything. The phrase "ping-pong diplomacy" was coined by the Western press almost immediately.

events.label: The Gang of Four
events.description: The Gang of Four was the Shanghai-based radical faction — Jiang Qing (Mao's wife), Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen — that controlled propaganda and culture during the late Cultural Revolution and fought savagely to prevent any retreat from revolutionary politics as Mao declined.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The name "Gang of Four" was reportedly coined by Mao himself in a private rebuke to Jiang Qing's faction — which meant that when Hua Guofeng used it after Mao's death to justify their arrest, he could claim he was acting on Mao's own words. Jiang Qing had been a Shanghai film actress in the 1930s before marrying Mao; the Party had made Mao promise she would never hold political office, a promise that turned to ash in the Cultural Revolution. Wang Hongwen, the youngest member, was only 38 when the gang fell — a textile worker turned radical who had risen to be third in the Party hierarchy.

events.label: Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius
events.description: A 1973–74 political campaign that nominally attacked both the disgraced Lin Biao and the ancient philosopher Confucius was actually a coded radical assault on Zhou Enlai — with "Confucius" standing in for Zhou and his preference for order and hierarchy over permanent revolution.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The campaign was launched by Mao and Jiang Qing but was transparently aimed at Zhou, since Confucius's supposed sins (restoring old aristocratic order, prioritizing stability over transformation) mapped perfectly onto Zhou's political positions. Zhou, dying of cancer and politically untouchable, could not be attacked directly — so the radicals attacked a philosopher dead 2,400 years instead. The campaign fizzled partly because ordinary Chinese found the historical analogy absurd, and partly because Mao himself grew bored with it.

events.label: The Return of Deng Xiaoping
events.description: Deng Xiaoping — purged in 1966 for being a "capitalist roader" and sent to work in a tractor factory — was brought back to run day-to-day government in 1973 by Zhou Enlai, who needed a tough administrator, and began pushing the Four Modernizations before the Gang of Four had him expelled again in 1976.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Deng had already survived one major purge before 1966: he had been one of the Long March veterans who had quietly disagreed with Mao during the Great Leap Forward. During his Cultural Revolution exile he was sent to work in a factory in Jiangxi province; his son Deng Pufang was thrown from a window by Red Guards and paralyzed for life. Deng was rehabilitated not once but twice — purged in 1966, returned in 1973, purged again in 1976, returned for good in 1977 — a resilience that made him the defining figure of post-Mao China.

events.label: The Four Modernizations
events.description: The Four Modernizations — reforming agriculture, industry, national defense, and science and technology — were Zhou Enlai's program for dragging China back from the edge of the Cultural Revolution's economic wreckage, and they became Deng Xiaoping's governing manifesto after 1978.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Zhou had actually first articulated the four goals as early as 1963, but they were politically radioactive during the Cultural Revolution (which treated economic pragmatism as ideological betrayal). The program was formally adopted only after Mao's death in 1977, framed as "rejuvenating China's economy." Deng later added the concept of "xiaokang" (a moderately prosperous society) as a concrete target — a phrase borrowed from Confucius, of all sources, signaling how completely the radical Maoist vocabulary had been abandoned.

events.label: The Tangshan Earthquake
events.description: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck the industrial city of Tangshan, Hebei, at 3:42 in the morning on July 28, 1976, collapsing 85 percent of the city's buildings in minutes and killing at least 242,469 people by official count — likely over 300,000, making it arguably the deadliest earthquake of the 20th century.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The earthquake struck before dawn when most residents were asleep, which is why the death toll was so catastrophic — there was essentially no warning and no chance to evacuate. In keeping with Maoist self-reliance doctrine, China refused all foreign disaster aid, a decision that likely cost additional lives. The official death toll was suppressed for years and only published in 1979; the true figure is still debated. Coming just two months before Mao's death, the quake reinforced the ancient Mandate of Heaven logic: Heaven was clearly withdrawing its favor.

events.label: The Arrest of the Gang of Four
events.description: On October 6, 1976 — less than a month after Mao's death — Premier Hua Guofeng and Defense Minister Ye Jianying had the Gang of Four arrested in a coordinated operation, ending the Cultural Revolution by coup and opening China to the reforms Deng Xiaoping would carry out.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The arrest was pulled off at a Politburo meeting the four were summoned to attend — a classic Party trap. Jiang Qing reportedly screamed that she had only been "carrying out Chairman Mao's orders." All four were put on trial in 1980–81 in a televised proceeding; Jiang Qing was defiant throughout, shouting at her accusers, and was sentenced to death (later commuted to life imprisonment). She died in custody in 1991. The trial was explicitly designed to draw a line between Mao (whose "70% good, 30% bad" verdict the Party announced) and the Cultural Revolution's worst crimes, which were pinned on the Gang.

events.label: The Stilwell Crisis
events.description: Roosevelt's push to put the American general Joseph Stilwell in command of China's armies collided with Chiang Kai-shek, who saw an overbearing foreigner and demanded his recall. Roosevelt granted it in October 1944, souring Washington on the Nationalists just as the postwar order was being decided.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Stilwell ran the China-Burma-India theater and privately called Chiang "the Peanut." In the summer of 1944, as Japan's Ichigo offensive tore through Nationalist China, George Marshall pushed Roosevelt to hand Stilwell command of all of China's armies, the Communists included. Roosevelt's blunt demand, delivered to Chiang in person, backfired: Chiang demanded Stilwell's recall, got it, and Stilwell was replaced by Albert Wedemeyer that October. Stilwell's acid account of a regime hoarding its strength rather than fighting helped shape the later American "who lost China" recriminations.
